LOS ÁNGELES - La temporada baja ha llegado antes de lo previsto para los Dodgers.
Antes de haber asimilado por completo la derrota del jueves por la noche (6-4) ante los Cerveceros en el Juego 4 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional —resultado que puso fin a su temporada y a su intento de lograr un tercer título consecutivo—, los Dodgers tuvieron que afrontar la realidad de que probablemente se avecinan cambios en el equipo.
Los Dodgers perderán a nueve jugadores debido a la agencia libre, un grupo encabezado por la figura más destacada del mercado, Tarik Skubal. Los otros jugadores que pronto serán agentes libres son el venezolano Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández, Evan Phillips, Alex Vesia, Blake Treinen, Eric Lauer, Kris Bubic y el venezolano Brusdar Graterol.
Gran parte del núcleo del equipo de Los Ángeles permanecerá intacto en el futuro previsible, por lo que la ventana competitiva no se está cerrando; sin embargo, este podría ser un periodo de transición entre una era del béisbol de los Dodgers y otra.
"Nunca puedes pensar que este es el final", dijo Rojas, quien permanecerá en la organización desempeñando un papel en el desarrollo de jugadores. "Y conozco muy bien a esta organización; no se conformarán con esta derrota".
A lo largo de 14 participaciones consecutivas en la postemporada, los Dodgers han encontrado formas fluidas de incorporar talento joven a sus plantillas para complementar a su núcleo de veteranos experimentados. Ese proceso ya ha comenzado con el dominicano Josue De Paula —el prospecto número 4 a nivel general según MLB Pipeline—, así como con el receptor suplente Dalton Rushing y el jugador de cuadro Alex Freeland.
No obstante, es posible que los Dodgers deban adoptar un enfoque más deliberado para asignar roles más destacados a sus jugadores jóvenes de cara al futuro, lo que dará lugar a decisiones interesantes durante esta temporada baja.
"No conocemos el futuro", comentó el dominicano Teóscar Hernández. "Pero algo que sabemos es que nos preocupamos los unos por los otros, nos cuidamos mutuamente y nos apoyamos durante todo el año... Este grupo es realmente especial, no por lo que hemos logrado en los últimos dos años y en este, sino simplemente por la unión que tenemos".
A continuación, un vistazo a algunas de las decisiones más importantes sobre el roster que deberán tomar los Dodgers durante esta temporada baja:
¿Participarán en la puja por Skubal?
Los Dodgers se desprendieron de dos prospectos clasificados entre los 100 mejores —el abridor listo para las Grandes Ligas River Ryan y el jardinero Zyhir Hope—, además del lanzador derecho Brady Smith, a cambio de contar con Skubal por un periodo de hasta tres meses. No fueron el único equipo dispuesto a hacer una gran inversión por un talento del calibre de Skubal, y lo mismo ocurrirá cuando este llegue al mercado de agentes libres por primera vez.
Skubal ganó su caso de arbitraje salarial contra los Tigres la temporada baja pasada, obteniendo un salario récord de US$32 millones. Se espera ampliamente que consiga la mayor cantidad de dinero garantizado jamás otorgada a un lanzador en la agencia libre, superando el contrato de 12 años y US$325 millones de Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
En su año previo a la agencia libre, Skubal se perdió seis semanas tras someterse a una cirugía en el codo izquierdo, pero aun así completó otra campaña sólida, registrando una marca de 12-7 y una efectividad de 2.72 en 26 aperturas con los Tigres y los Dodgers. Prefirió no hablar sobre su futuro inmediatamente después de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional (SCLN).
"Sí, realmente no voy a hacer comentarios sobre mi futuro", dijo Skubal. "El día de hoy es una porquería, ya sabes, y en eso es en lo que estoy pensando ahora mismo".
Aun así, Skubal expresó su agradecimiento por el tiempo que pasó con los Dodgers.
"Una organización increíble, compañeros increíbles, una afición increíble", dijo. "Es un honor llevar las letras 'L.A.' en el pecho y en la gorra".
¿Cómo le darán tiempo de juego para De Paula?
En septiembre, De Paula hizo que el salto de Doble-A a las Grandes Ligas pareciera sencillo, impresionando tanto a los Dodgers que logró entrar en el roster de postemporada como opción de bateador emergente. Sin embargo, su limitación radicaba en que el equipo de Grandes Ligas lo veía únicamente como bateador designado, una posición ocupada por Shohei Ohtani.
"Creo que la mejora que Josue mostró en los jardines entre 2025 y 2026 es real", comentó el mes pasado Andrew Friedman, presidente de operaciones de béisbol. "Y para nosotros, se trata de dar otro gran paso de cara a 2027. Él tiene las herramientas y la capacidad para lograrlo".
Con el tiempo, los Dodgers tendrán que poner a De Paula a jugar en los jardines. No obstante, sus jardineros titulares —Teóscar Hernández, el cubano Andy Pages y Kyle Tucker— tienen contrato vigente hasta la próxima temporada.
Si los Dodgers consideran que De Paula está listo para ser jugador titular habitual, eso probablemente implicaría, como mínimo, limitar el tiempo de juego de Hernández. También podría darse una medida más drástica: buscar un equipo interesado en asumir la última temporada garantizada de su contrato de tres años y US$66 millones.
Otra opción sería que De Paula comenzara la temporada en Triple-A, donde podría trabajar en su defensa en un entorno de menor presión.
¿Qué jugadores veteranos clave regresarán?
Entre los agentes libres inminentes, algunas de las bajas más significativas en cuanto a liderazgo serían Kiké Hernández, Phillips, Vesia y Treinen. El bullpen ciertamente podría tener hueco para lanzadores de situaciones críticas como Phillips y Vesia, pero el encaje de Hernández entre los jugadores de posición no está tan claro.
Hernández, el propio "Mr. October" de los Dodgers, tuvo una temporada regular marcada por las lesiones. Tampoco estuvo a la altura de su habitual rendimiento en postemporada, conectando apenas un jonrón solitario en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional (SDLN) como único imparable. Es una figura importante en el vestuario y, aunque le encantaría volver a Los Ángeles, sabe que sus necesidades y las del equipo deben coincidir durante la agencia libre.
"Me encantaría intentarlo una vez más, tratar de ganar otro", dijo Hernández. "Pero realmente no sé qué va a pasar. Espero volver y, si no es así, espero poder jugar en un equipo ganador".

LOS ANGELES — The past two years, the Dodgers’ season ended with parades and calls to “Run it back” for the next season.
After their four-game sweep in the National League Championship Series at the hands of a younger, hungrier Milwaukee Brewers team ended the dream of a ‘three-peat,’ how realistic is it to head into 2027 with the same core – the oldest position player group in MLB for the past four years?
“That’s not my job. I play first base,” said Freddie Freeman, at 37 the oldest returning player on the Dodgers’ roster (infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement and relief pitcher Blake Treinen, who suffered a shoulder injury late in the season, is a free agent).
“We’ve got a great group of guys. We’ve accomplished a lot of things. We came up short in these four days. But we’ll see where the wind blows this offseason, what happens, what it looks like, what baseball looks like.”
The winds of change could be coming. As Freeman alluded to, the anticipated showdown between MLB’s owners and the players’ union over the next Collective Bargaining Agreement could force the biggest changes in the Dodgers’ future. If the owners are able to get the salary cap or other payroll restrictions they are aiming for, the Dodgers might be forced to change their roster by shedding payroll.
Also looming over the team’s future are the ongoing legal and financial difficulties surrounding principal owner Mark Walter that threaten to eat into the Dodgers’ enormous financial advantages.
Threatening the franchise’s plans to keep its “Golden Era” going more directly, though, is the aging roster. The Brewers certainly made the Dodgers look old in the four-game NLCS sweep.
“I don’t know what you can really say to that. That’s just people’s opinions of what that is,” Freeman said before Game 4. “We do know we have an older team. That doesn’t mean we’re old and we’re playing bad because we’re old. We’re just not playing that great, in my mind.
“But that’s people’s opinions. I can’t change your opinion because we are, in this game, a little bit older than everybody else. I don’t feel old.”
Nonetheless, Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman acknowledged awareness – if not overt concern – about the aging core on the team’s roster.
“Yeah, we’ve talked about this a lot,” Friedman said before the start of the NLCS. “With where we are in the success cycle, the success we have had, we have done the opposite of being flippant about it. ‘Oh, it’s great that we won. Now we can put our feet up.’ For us, it’s about pressing the advantage we have right now.
“We have a very talented core, and while a good number of them are getting up there in years, the experience, the way they prepare, the way they play the game, we feel like is a real competitive advantage. So we’ve been aggressive to supplement around that group, all the while pouring ourselves into our next wave.”
The Dodgers’ farm system is indeed as strong as any in MLB. They subtracted two Top 100 prospects (outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-hander River Ryan) in order to trade for pitcher Tarik Skubal in August and still have five more led by outfielder Josue De Paula.
De Paula made the jump from Double-A to the majors in September and showed his readiness in that brief audition. The Dodgers will have to make room for him in their 2027 plan.
That won’t be easy and it’s difficult to see how the Dodgers can get younger in 2027 other than around the margins where Kiké Hernandez acknowledged Game 4 of the NLCS might be his last with the Dodgers and Rojas made it clear, talking to the team after the game and saying he was retiring. He is expected to stay with the organization in some capacity, likely in player development.
“This is it as a player. That was my last game playing. That was the last time I put these cleats on and this uniform on as a player,” Rojas said, still in full uniform long after the game ended Thursday night. “From now on, I’m going to start thinking about what’s going to happen in my life as a baseball person other than being a player. I want to start my career on the other side of this business, and I’m looking forward to doing it here with the Los Angeles Dodgers as well.
“I’m ready to move on and start the next chapter of my career.”
Hernandez isn’t ready to stop playing. But he knows it might not be in Los Angeles next year.
“I mean, I love this place. I’ve played for three other teams, but every time I look at my career I kind of obviously go back to this place,” the 35-year-old Hernandez said. “I feel like I have a lot left. … I would love to be back. I would love to have one more try, trying to win another one. But I don’t really know what’s going to happen. I hope I’m back, and if I’m not I hope that I get to play for a winning team.”
Seven other Dodgers will become free agents this winter, most prominently bullpen stalwarts Alex Vesia and Evan Phillips and Skubal. Four others – Freeman, outfielder Teoscar Hernandez, third baseman Max Muncy and utility player Hyeseong Kim – are entering the final year of their contracts in 2027, though all but Freeman have club options for 2028.
If the Dodgers are going to change things by their own hand (as opposed to CBA mandate), Teoscar Hernandez clearly has a target on his back as the most likely Dodger to be traded this winter, clearing left field for De Paula. But the Dodgers have largely painted themselves into a corner with this roster. Freeman, shortstop Mookie Betts, catcher Will Smith, center fielder Andy Pages, right fielder Kyle Tucker, two-way star Shohei Ohtani and Muncy, each a year older, are all likely to be in the starting lineup on Opening Day 2027 – whenever that might be.
“I have no idea,” Muncy said of the potential for changes before next season. “That’s for people above me to make those decisions and it’s for me to show up next year, ready to go with whatever group we’ve got. There will come a time when we think about next year. But that’s not at this moment.”
Showing up at Camelback Ranch next spring with the same core is not necessarily a bad thing. Even with only minimal changes, the Dodgers will enter 2027 as the favorites in the National League West once again and a 15th consecutive postseason berth would bring another chance to win the “crapshoot” October has become.
But it also brings this Dodger core closer to “the cliff” Friedman has talked about avoiding.
“It’s tricky because you have to find the right balance,” he said. “It’s hard to transition young players onto your roster. It’s a hard adjustment from Triple-A to the major-league level. We’ve done it some over the years. Some guys we haven’t had the patience long enough to kind of see it through (perhaps an allusion to infielder Miguel Vargas, now an All-Star for the Chicago White Sox).
“That’s the challenge we have with the expectations we have. So we have to be mindful of having a really high standard but also transitioning some of our young players. We’ve seen it some, Andy Pages is featured prominently for us, Will Smith, Alex Freeland got a lot of opportunities this year. Dalton Rushing was a big part when Will missed time. And then late in the year we saw with Josue De Paula.
“We’ve got a lot of guys coming after that as well. So for us it’s about almost having a split personality – to do everything we can to maximize our chances of winning with our major-league roster, and the other side of our personality is pouring ourselves into doing everything we can to have as much talent coming, and we feel really good about that part as well.”

LOS ANGELES (AP) — After their earliest postseason exit in three years, the Los Angeles Dodgers head into the offseason facing uncertainty over next year.
Shohei Ohtani was dogged by injuries to his left knee and right biceps over the second half and into the playoffs that rendered him ineffective at the plate. The two-way superstar also didn't pitch after the All-Star break.
Whether Ohtani needs offseason surgery remains to be seen, although he acknowledged it's possible after Thursday's loss to the Brewers that completed Milwaukee's sweep of the NL Championship Series. If he does, would the recovery bleed into the start of next season?
A potential MLB lockout is looming with the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1. Team owners have proposed a salary cap — something the sport has never had — and the players' union has adamantly rejected the idea.
A work stoppage would give Ohtani extra time to heal, although during such time the Dodgers would be cut off from communicating with any player, leaving Ohtani to rehab either from possible surgery or from his injuries on his own.
Communication between Ohtani and the team on his health during the season was “awesome,” Andrew Friedman, president of baseball operations, said last month, but he added: “The fully sharing exactly how he's feeling, maybe not so awesome.”
Ohtani said he plans to resume pitching next year, when he'll turn 33 in July. He's already had two Tommy John surgeries.
“What he’s doing is unprecedented, and it takes a real toll,” Friedman said. “And as you get older, I think us just being very dialed is going to be really important.”
Roster turnover is likely, even without big changes in MLB spending rules
The Dodgers had baseball's second-highest opening day payroll this year at $323.3 million, behind the New York Mets at $358.4 million. If a salary cap were to be imposed, the Dodgers' spending would be constrained when play resumes.
Some of the roster could look different next year, too, with nine players set to become free agents after the World Series, led by two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is expected to command a huge deal.
The Dodgers acquired Skubal from Detroit just before the trade deadline in August. The left-hander was 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 regular-season games for his new team. In the postseason, he was 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA and 14 Ks. Skubal didn't want to discuss his future Thursday, although he expressed enthusiasm for the organization, his teammates and the fans.
Advertisement
Other impending free agents are infielder Miguel Rojas, utility player Kiké Hernández, and relievers Kris Bubic, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Evan Phillips, Blake Treinen and Alex Vesia.
As expected, Rojas announced his retirement Thursday, saying, “This is it, guys. That was my last game played.” He'll still be around, though, to work in a player development role.
Dodgers add a bit of youth with De Paula
The Dodgers got a glimpse of the future when they promoted Josue De Paula directly from Double-A to the majors in September. His energy and at-bats at designated hitter during Ohtani's stint on the injured list made an impression, and the 21-year-old was added to the postseason roster as a pinch-hitter.
The team will look to De Paula to further improve as an outfielder in 2027, although finding playing time for him will be challenging given the trio of veteran starters: Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker. De Paula is also blocked at DH by Ohtani.
“I think the experience he got being up here and watching what our guys do on a daily basis just helped connect some dots for him,” Friedman said. “And so, physically, he is capable of being a good corner outfielder, and we’re going to continue to tap into that.”
Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Ohtani, Tucker, Max Muncy and Will Smith will remain the Dodgers' veteran core. But some supporting players could be offloaded, like Kiké Hernández. Playing on a one-year deal, the 35-year-old was limited to 41 games while recovering from injuries and he didn't provide his usual postseason pop.
Manager Dave Roberts refused to blame an aging lineup for getting swept by the Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were three more than the Dodgers.
“We got beat,” he said. “There’s no because we’re too old or whatever. Every facet of the game, if you kind of unpack it, we were bested.”
There's drama off the field, too.
Owner Mark Walter was noticeably absent from the team's playoff games. He is facing multiple federal investigations into his business empire for possible financial improprieties involving insurance companies he controls. Walter has denied any wrongdoing. Since August, he sold his controlling interest in the Los Angeles Lakers and last month he unloaded his share in Chelsea of the Premier League.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers dynasty is over, or has at least hit a major bump in the road. Thursday's Game 4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers completed the four-game sweep and sent the two-time defending World Series champions home for the winter. Los Angeles' season is over, as is its stretch of eight consecutive postseason series wins dating back to 2024.
There is no getting around it: The Dodgers looked old in the NLCS. They are old too. Weighed by playing time, they had baseball's oldest collection of position players this season. Will Smith is 31. Shohei Ohtani is 32. Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernández are 34. Freddie Freeman is 37. The team's core hitters are getting long in the tooth. It was obvious in the NLCS.
That said, the Dodgers remain extremely talented and have the resources (money and tradeable prospects) to improve their roster in the offseason, and again contend in 2027. As bad as they looked in the NLCS, there is no reason to think the Dodgers won't be among baseball's best teams next year -- and on the short list of legitimate World Series contenders.
Here now are three questions facing the Dodgers following their unceremonious NLCS sweep.
1. What is Shohei Ohtani's future?
The two-way star was hindered by health for a large chunk of 2026
In fact, let's talk about his future both short- and long-term. Ohtani was clearly diminished late in the regular season and into the postseason. He played through knee and biceps injuries and simply did not look like himself at the plate. His swing was all arms and there was little hard contact. Before his second-inning home run in Game 4 on Thursday, Ohtani hadn't gone deep since Aug. 18. His power vanished.
Here is Ohtani's expected slugging percentage, which is based on contact quality (exit velocity, launch angle, etc.), throughout this season. It slipped significantly late in the year:
Ohtani did not pitch after July 3 and had a start-and-stop in late August. He rehabbed his injuries, threw bullpen sessions and live batting practice, then had to shut it down before getting back on a mound in a game. Ohtani was playing like his usual MVP self until his injuries popped up in the second half. Once that happened, his season began to circle the drain.
The Dodgers now face two questions with Ohtani. One, does he need offseason surgery on the knee and/or biceps? And if he does need surgery, will the recovery cut into his 2027? Keep in mind that it is a near certainty there will be a lockout this offseason once the CBA expires on Dec. 1, and teams will be banned from communicating with their players. Ohtani would have to rehab on his own, without the team's input.
"It's hard to tell" if he'll require surgery, Ohtani said through an interpreter after Thursday's loss. He does, however, plan to pitch next season, he said.
Offseason surgery is the short-term question. Long-term, regardless of what he said in the shadow of the NLCS sweep, are Ohtani's days as a pitcher numbered? This has been a question since Day 1 of Ohtani's MLB career. His ability to be and remain a two-way player has long been doubted, but he has kept doing it, even if there have been some speed bumps along the way. Ohtani has made a career of doing what people said he couldn't.
The man is 32 now, though. He'll turn 33 next summer and the physical ailments (the knee, the biceps, two UCL surgeries, etc.) are beginning to add up. At some point, Ohtani won't be able to continue as a two-way player, and with each passing season, that point draws closer. Are we there now? Is this it? Is this the end of Ohtani's time as a pitcher? It could be, sure.
My guess is that Ohtani will continue to pitch next season and the Dodgers will happily let him because there is so much value to be gained even if he throws only 75 innings a year. You can't be as good as Ohtani without being stubborn. He's been stubborn in that he insists on playing both ways, and he has continued to do it well. I don't see him dropping it this winter.
It should surprise no one if Ohtani comes out next year, hits 40 home runs, makes 15 ace-caliber starts and wins his fifth MVP unanimously. Do not forget that he was playing at that level as recently as July. The recovery times for the knee and biceps injuries are an offseason question, for sure, and the bottom line is the "will he continue to pitch?" questions will always exist.
2. Will they move on from some longtime stalwarts?
Could the Dodgers say goodbye to Teoscar Hernández or some other familiar names?
The Dodgers are locked into so much of their core: Betts, Freeman, Ohtani, Smith, Kyle Tucker, etc. They aren't going anywhere. That said, there are a few members of the supporting cast, players who have been around for all three recent World Series wins, who might have to be shown the door this offseason for the sake of diversifying the lineup and getting younger and more athletic.
Finding a taker for the final season of Teoscar Hernández's contract and then plugging the precocious Josue De Paula into left field next season is a worthwhile move. It's difficult because Hernández is popular in the clubhouse, but, on the field, De Paula figures to give the Dodgers a better chance to win ballgames moving forward. (De Paula is a poor defender, but so is Hernández.)
The Enrique Hernández era has run its course. He hasn't been even an average regular-season player since 2022, and, for all his postseason heroics, he's barely scraping a .600 OPS in the last two Octobers. Tommy Edman is a better version of the same player. There's no need to carry both on the roster, plus Edman's injuries suggest a smaller role is needed. Less could be more.
Max Muncy stayed healthy this season, hit 29 homers and posted 4.1 WAR, and is owed an affordable $10 million in 2027. Plus, it's a bad offseason to need an infielder. The free-agent market is very thin and you're not likely to find better than Muncy on the trade market. Still, he is 36. Keeping Muncy is justifiable, but it also makes sense to explore alternatives. It never hurts to look.
Blake Treinen has not been healthy and effective at the same time in two years. Alex Vesia's fastball sat 91-92 mph over these last few weeks. Both are free agents and the Dodgers have so many young hard-throwers in Triple-A that I think it's worth turning the page and injecting some younger arms into the bullpen. Evan Phillips may be in this camp, too.
Then again, who am I to doubt the Dodgers and their process? Disappointing NLCS aside, they have been baseball's most successful team of the 2020s, and if they want to remain in the Hernández and Muncy and Treinen business, I won't say they're wrong. It does appear that things are getting a bit stale, though. Incorporating youth would be sensible, and it isn't difficult to find ways to do it.
3. Will they retain Tarik Skubal?
It will cost a lot to keep the trade deadline addition atop the rotation
There's no sense in asking if the Dodgers can retain Tarik Skubal. Of course they can. They are baseball's biggest spenders and he is a Scott Boras client. Typically, all you need to do to get a Boras client is make the biggest offer, which the Dodgers can do. Maybe there's a salary cap that changes the equation. Based on what we know right now, yes, the Dodgers can, of course, re-sign Skubal.
Will they is a different matter. Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto will return next season. Ohtani could be back on the mound as well, as he indicated is the plan. Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski both pitched well for long stretches this year and are among the very best No. 5 starter options in the game. Gavin Stone, the team's 2024 innings leader, should return from shoulder surgery as well.
There is never a bad time to sign a pitcher like Skubal, and the Dodgers, with their World Series window still open, are well-positioned to bring him back. They have the money, they can easily clear rotation space, and all indications are that Skubal enjoyed his time with the team after coming over the trade deadline. This feels like a match made in free-agent heaven.
Now it's just a matter of whether the Dodgers can get it done. Perhaps a salary cap or increased competitive balance tax penalties limit their spending; maybe they opt to spread their money around to multiple players; maybe another team just won't be denied. The Dodgers don't absolutely need Skubal. Re-signing him would up their odds of returning to the World Series, though, and help ensure their dynasty didn't end on Thursday night.
For his part, Skubal declined to comment on his impending decision after Game 4.
"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," Skubal said, via MLB.com. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."

LOS ANGELES (AP) — Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning, Milwaukee's brilliant bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 on Thursday in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to earn their first World Series trip since 1982.
No. 9 hitter David Hamilton's two-out solo shot off Edwin Díaz gave the Brewers a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season.
“We got down early tonight and we were like, it’s going to be a great story,” Brewers captain Christian Yelich said. “We’re going to come back and win this. Like, stay together, start chipping away. And that’s exactly what they did.”
Aaron Ashby pitched three scoreless innings for a save as the Brewers erased a four-run deficit to win their first NL pennant and second overall. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise made its only previous World Series appearance 44 years ago, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals.
Shohei Ohtani's first home run this postseason helped put the Dodgers ahead 4-0 in the second inning before the Brewers came back to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending World Series champions a year after getting swept by Los Angeles in the NLCS.
“They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we’ve got a bunch of gamers — and the gamers won this week,” Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said.
The Dodgers' goal of a three-peat — not done since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 and never by a National League team — died with their anemic offense and injuries to Ohtani and others on their aging roster.
“I'm not used to those consolation speeches,” manager Dave Roberts said. “The thing about sports that we all love is no matter how much you prepare, you want it, there’s no guarantees.”
After topping the majors with 103 wins during the regular season, Milwaukee became the first major league club to finish a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason.
The Brewers also are the first team to sweep a best-of-seven postseason series in which it trailed in every game.
“There was never a doubt in that dugout what was going to happen tonight. We knew we were going to win that game,” said first baseman Jake Bauers, the NLCS MVP.
With the score tied 4-all, Mitchell fell behind 0-2 before reliever Tanner Scott threw three straight balls for a full count. Mitchell’s 409-foot leadoff drive to center field — the first homer of his career on an 0-2 count — put the Brewers ahead for the first time. Mitchell also homered in their 6-2 victory Wednesday.
“It’s absolutely surreal," Mitchell said. "You talk about the battle-tested Brewers. We went down early and the belief in that dugout got stronger and stronger.”
The Brewers’ bullpen coolly turned away multiple threats when the Dodgers had the potential tying run on base.
Winning pitcher JoJo Romero struck out Max Muncy with Kyle Tucker at third to end the sixth.
With one out in the seventh and a runner on third, Ashby struck out Ohtani swinging before Mookie Betts grounded out to end the inning. Will Smith doubled to right with one out in the eighth and was safe at third when the ball got away from Sal Frelick for an error before Ashby got Tucker to fly out and Teoscar Hernández to strike out.
“Playing with that chip on our shoulder,” Ashby said. “You don’t ever know what to expect going into a series like that last year (against the Dodgers). You don’t know how bad it can be, and then it was as bad as it was. And we came out and we survived, and we came back this year, and those guys played their tails off.”
The Brewers tied it in the fifth, when the Dodgers bullpen issued four walks and Milwaukee stole two bases. Hamilton’s single chased starter Tyler Glasnow and scored Frelick, who walked and stole second, to pull Milwaukee to 4-3.
Alex Vesia came in and promptly walked Brice Turang and William Contreras to load the bases. Vesia then walked Bauers with two outs to force in Hamilton with the tying run.
Glasnow retired his first 10 batters — six on strikeouts — before the Brewers got to him in the fourth. Turang walked, Contreras hit a ground-rule double and Bauers followed with another ground-rule double that closed Milwaukee to 4-2.

LOS ANGELES — With the score tied at four in the top of the sixth inning, Tanner Scott threw a fastball down the middle and Garrett Mitchell crushed it.
As the ball soared over the centre field wall at Dodger Stadium, reality set in for the two-time defending champions and their fans: their reign atop MLB might be ending. And a few innings later, when Aaron Ashby retired Kiké Hernandez for the final out of a 6-4 win in Game 4 of the NLCS, it was all over.
There were late chances to score Kyle Tucker from second and Will Smith from third, but in the end the Dodgers failed.
They’re a great team, but not the best team in baseball anymore, or even the best team in the National League. That honour goes to the Milwaukee Brewers, who secured the pennant with a sweep of the Dodgers thanks to Mitchell’s big swing, some tenacious rallies in the middle innings and impressive relief pitching.
The win overshadowed a dramatic home run from Shohei Ohtani and disappointed 49,104 fans still hoping for a third straight championship. Instead, it’s Milwaukee who will represent the National League in the World Series in a battle of small markets against either Cleveland or Tampa Bay.
All series, the Brewers outplayed the Dodgers. They hit more home runs, they played better defence and they pitched better. And really, that should come as no surprise. This team has reached the post-season eight of the last nine seasons, including each of the last four NL Central titles.
But still, the Dodgers are baseball’s preeminent team, so when Shohei Ohtani demolished a Dustin May cutter to give the Dodgers an early 4-0 lead, their path to victory seemed to open up again. As the ball soared into the right-field bleachers, Ohtani bounced backwards towards first base and yelled at his teammates in the third-base dugout. It may be the most emotion he’s ever shown on a big-league field.
Considering the context, Ohtani’s home run was all the more significant. Just two days ago, there was talk of benching him given his middling performance and knee and biceps injuries. Then came a stellar performance in Game 3 and his Game 4 home run, the first one he’s hit since August 18.
But aside from Ohtani’s big swing, the Dodgers simply didn’t have answers offensively. No one else homered in the NLCS. In fact, they had just five other extra-base hits this series — all doubles. A team known for its high-powered offence had produced backup-catcher type numbers when it counted most.
They needed to hit or see their season end, no in-between. And they didn’t hit, so their season ended.
The Brewers, on the other hand, managed just enough offence. David Hamilton added a late home run and breakout star Jake Bauers drove in three, including two with a pivotal double in the fourth inning. All series, they found answers against the Dodgers team that allowed the fewest runs in MLB this regular season.
Oddly enough, this will be the first time the Brewers represent the National League in the World Series. When they made it in 1982, they were still an American League team and lost to the Cardinals in seven games.
The Dodgers were seeking the first MLB three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees and only the fifth in MLB history (Athletics 1972-74; Yankees 1949-53; Yankees 1936-39). Instead, they’ll turn their attention to the off-season, with Hernandez, Miguel Rojas, Alex Vesia and, most notably, Tarik Skubal all headed for free agency.
Before then, the Brewers will participate in a World Series featuring two of MLB’s lowest payrolls, undermining the narrative that MLB needs a salary cap for small-market teams to compete. The Brewers didn’t just beat the Dodgers, they dominated them thanks to elite player acquisition, strong player development and a strong team culture.
Soon enough, more tests await the Brewers. First, though, it’s time for a well deserved celebration.

LOS ANGELES -- Major League Baseball honored Jackie Robinson on Wednesday with every player, coach and umpire wearing his No. 42 to mark the 79th anniversary of the infielder breaking the sport's color barrier.
Robinson made his debut for the Brooklyn Dodgers on April 15, 1947. He went on to win Rookie of the Year honors and become a six-time All-Star and the 1949 National League MVP. He played in six World Series and won his only championship in 1955 with the Dodgers.
"Every player of color who now enjoys our great sport, they owe it to this man," said Bob Kendrick, president of the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum in Kansas City, Missouri.
Robinson made his pro debut with the Kansas City Monarchs of the Negro Leagues in 1945. He was there five months before Dodgers general manager Branch Rickey interviewed him for possible selection to Brooklyn's International League farm club. Rickey wanted to make sure Robinson could withstand the racial antagonism without reacting angrily.
"What he did was incredibly difficult under some of the most harsh circumstances you could ever imagine," Kendrick said. "He had to go out there and deal not only with the racial hatred but he was carrying 21 million Black folks on his back when he walked across those lines. Had he failed, an entire race of people would have failed. That's an enormous amount of pressure. How he did it with such grace, class and dignity is absolutely incredible. And no, we should never forget Jackie Robinson."
The Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets gathered around the center-field statue of Robinson stealing home at Dodger Stadium. Among the Dodgers were Tyler Glasnow, Teoscar Hernandez, Will Smith, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia and Will Klein. Shohei Ohtani, who has attended previously, was not there ahead of pitching against the Mets later.
"A special day, especially for me as a Latino. I wouldn't be here if it wasn't because of him," Mets manager Carlos Mendoza said. "Talk about dealing with pressure at this level, imagine what he dealt with back in the day."
The Dodgers' Dave Roberts, one of just two Black managers currently in the majors, told the teams Robinson would be proud that they reflect his dream and vision of what equality and unity would look like.
"My ask is that we remember how we got here," Roberts said.
In New York, Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. wore his pinstripe pants loose and blousy and rolled at the knees the way many players did in the 1940s, including Robinson.
A video commemorating Robinson and narrated by former Yankees pitcher CC Sabathia was played on the stadium scoreboard before the team's game against the Los Angeles Angels.
"You look at the diversity in our game as far as now, worldwide, and Jackie was the start of opening those doors to not just Black players being able to play but Latin America," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said, "and now we have people from all over the globe playing this, and Jackie was the start of all that."
In Pittsburgh, Pirates manager Don Kelly said, "It doesn't seem like one day is enough to really give back to Jackie and what he meant to baseball and to people."
Two of Robinson's granddaughters joined the teams at Dodger Stadium, not far from Robinson's adopted hometown of Pasadena. He was a four-sport star at Pasadena Junior College before going on to UCLA, where the Georgia native was better known for football than baseball.
Last year, a historical marker honoring the Robinson family was unveiled by the city of Pasadena at their former home.
"We're really carrying the legacy now and it's an incredible honor," said granddaughter Ayo Robinson, whose father, David, is Robinson's youngest son. "It's a weight that feels good because it keeps you grounded in what is so important. I feel like the legacy is just as important today as it has ever been."
Robinson's widow, Rachel, turns 104 in July. She lives in New York and still visits the Jackie Robinson Museum.
"She's the strong matriarch of our family, surrounded by love and intention to continue to allow her to live a life that she wanted," said granddaughter Sonya Pankey Robinson, whose father was Jackie Robinson Jr.
Also on hand in Los Angeles were recipients of scholarships from the Jackie Robinson Foundation.
For the first time in at least two decades, the percentage of Black players on Opening Day rosters increased this season. Major League Baseball says 6.8% of players on Opening Day rosters, injured lists and the restricted list were Black, up from 6.2% at the start of the 2025 season and 6.0% at the start of 2024.
"He's an icon," Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy said of Robinson. "To take this day and make it something special says a lot about the character of the game."br/]

The Los Angeles Dodgers are two games away from being eliminated at the hands of the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series.
With right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto having pitched in Game 2, the current state of affairs is far from where fans expected the Dodgers to be as the series heads back to LA. The 2025 World Series MVP lasted just 2.2 innings on Monday in an uncharacteristic one-strikeout performance, but there was still tons of baseball to be played after his exit.
After left-hander Alex Vesia finished off the third inning with four pitches, one of last year's October standouts in Roki Sasaki trotted out to the mound to face the Brewers in the fourth.
Sasaki's October success last season, especially in multi-inning spots, is partially why manager Dave Roberts was in a position to explain himself for only having Sasaki out to throw one frame.
The man who opened up the bottom of the fifth inning for LA, southpaw Kris Bubic, recorded just two outs on 22 pitches, one of which was turned into a solo home run for Brewers catcher William Contreras to tie the game.
Despite Sasaki's resume, Roberts went with the left-hander, but revealed he was looking for far more than two outs from the former All-Star.
"To me, you're trying to cover six-plus innings," Roberts said. "For me, I felt Bubic had four out of five left-handed hitters, and that's a perfect spot for him. I knew they weren't going to for him, and you got Roki for an inning, and then you still have a guy — in my opinion, you've got a great spot for Bubic. Tries to go with the fastball up to Contreras and then hits a homer.
"That's a decision I made, and we just didn't — again, that's his lane to be able to go out there and throw up a zero."
After Bubic walked a batter to leave a man on first and second, Brock Stewart came in to end the inning. Instead of a fresh arm coming in for the bottom of the sixth, Stewart remained in the game. Three batters later, Contreras was back up to bat with a tie game, two on and one out.
Contreras hit the first pitch he saw 76.9 mph into the outfield grass to give his team the lead and Stewart was removed from the contest. Tanner Scott entered the game after him and promptly struck out the next two batters to get out of the inning.
Roberts was asked about why Stewart was in instead of Scott entering against an already hot Contreras.
"It just felt like trying to put Contreras on the ground," Roberts said. "Contreras didn't hit the ball hard. He flared it out to left field, drove in a run, and that's what they do."
Roberts continued to point out the differences between the kind of at-bats that the Brewers' brand is a byproduct of.
"I think for me just in total they saw a ton more pitches than we did," Roberts said. "They had much better at-bats than we did across the board top to bottom, and then they put the ball in play, created havoc, and that's what they do, and we didn't do that.
"That's the difference in the game. I think that there's certainly a lot to unpack, but they did what needed to do tonight."

MILWAUKEE — Billboards around town promote the Milwaukee Brewers with the slogan “Win Our Way.”
The Dodgers tried. It didn’t work.
They scored four runs without getting a hit with a runner in scoring position – or hitting a home run. But the Brewers outhit them 12-3 and the final 15 Dodgers batters were retired in order as the Brewers pulled away to a 7-4 victory on Monday in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series.
“They pitched well and they hit good,” Freddie Freeman said. “That’s the name of the game, and they did it better than us today.”
They did it twice in Milwaukee. The best-of-seven series now heads back to Los Angeles with the Dodgers trailing 2-0. Game 3 is Wednesday at 5 p.m. with Blake Snell scheduled to start for the Dodgers.
“Grind. Win one game at a time, one pitch at a time,” Mookie Betts said. “The mindset can’t really change. We can’t add more pressure. There’s already enough as it is. Keep it simple. One pitch at a time. Figure out a way to get a hit.”
They have played hard to get for the Dodgers this postseason. Through six games against the Atlanta Braves and Brewers, they are batting .193 (37 for 192) as a team and, most costly, 2 for 26 (.077) with runners in scoring position.
“I don’t have an answer why,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I know that they’ve got good arms. So do we. I think they’re just finding ways to win pitches better than we are. Sometimes you’ve got to find a way to get a base hit and those guys — there’s a lot of balls that weren’t hit hard tonight but found the outfield grass. That’s hitting.”
The Dodgers found ways to score without hitting early in Game 2.
The pesky, opportunistic Dodgers scored a run in the first inning without a hit. Betts drew a leadoff walk, moved to second on Freddie Freeman’s slow roller then third on a wild pitch and scored on a sacrifice fly by Teoscar Hernandez.
They scored again on a pair of singles and a wild pickoff throw by Brewers starting pitcher Logan Henderson who was more effective throwing home than he was to first base.
That came up again in the fifth inning. Kyle Tucker led off with a double and Tommy Edman tried to bunt him to third – you wanted bunts. Henderson did him one better, fielding the ball and throwing wildly to first base. Tucker scored on Henderson’s second error and Edman wound up scoring on a close play at the plate (confirmed by replay) on a sacrifice fly by Freeman.
Each of the runs either gave the Dodgers the lead or tied the game as the two teams played in a phone booth, never straying more than a run apart.
That was true, in part, because Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto was not sharp. He threw 75 pitches to get just two outs into the third inning. The Brewers swung at 33 of those pitches and only missed four times.
“He wasn’t as precise as he normally is,” Dodgers catcher Will Smith said. “I thought they did a really good job, not expanding out of the zone, taking advantage, especially up the middle.”
Two key decisions by Smith could have changed things, though.
On a 2-and-2 pitch to Brice Turang in the first inning, Yamamoto seemed to hit the outside corner with a cutter for strike three – or he didn’t. That was the call by home plate umpire Chris Segal. It might have been overturned by ABS but Smith did not challenge.
Two pitches later, Turang doubled. William Contreras drove him in with a single.
“Yeah, I went back and looked,” Smith said of the questionable call. “I don’t know if it clipped it or whatever. It was kind of early in the game. We kind of had him on the ropes where we could just get him out there.
“The walk one was a bummer but I guess it happens. It’s baseball.”
That came two innings later. The Brewers had a runner at second with one out when Yamamoto again appeared to hit the outside corner with a splitter on a full count to Turang. Segal called it a ball and Yamamoto appeared to gesture towards Smith that he wanted to challenge. Smith didn’t.
“That one was a splitter. It actually cut back a little bit,” Smith said. “I just saw it out (of the strike zone) and didn’t know if it came back enough or not.”
Two batters later, Jake Bauers won a 12-pitch battle with Yamamoto – the longest plate appearance against Yamamoto this season – fouling off six consecutive pitches before drawing a walk to load the bases.
“I was trying to work on the edge of the zone,” Yamamoto said through his interpreter. “And some pitches it was really good but he just stayed on it. He did a good job.”
Two pitches later, Christian Yelich stroked a two-run single through the middle, the first base hit off of a Yamamoto curveball since August 27 and the last pitch Yamamoto would throw in the game.
“That changed the game,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said of Bauers’ walk, adding that he was told the confrontation lasted seven minutes. “You think about that and what it does to a pitcher. He can get through an inning in less than seven minutes and he does all the time. He’s one of the best pitchers in the land. It was a great at-bat. I think a turning point, I really do.”
It started the Dodgers’ bullpen turning.
Roberts turned to Alex Vesia to finish off the third and gave the ball to Roki Sasaki for a scoreless fourth.
But then he took it away from the converted starter after just one inning and gave it to Kris Bubic with two lefties coming up in the fifth. In between them was Contreras and he tied the game with a solo home run off Bubic. The Dodgers never regained a lead.
“For me, I felt Bubic had 4 out of 5 left-handed hitters (coming up), and that’s a perfect spot for him,” Roberts said. “I knew they weren’t going to hit for them. You have Roki for an inning, and then you still have a guy — in my opinion, you’ve got a great spot for Bubic.
“That’s a decision I made, and we just didn’t — again, that’s his lane to be able to go out there and throw up a zero.”
The Brewers finally did things their way in the sixth inning against Brock Stewart.
He hit No. 9 hitter David Hamilton with a pitch. Hamilton went to second when Freeman mishandled a pickoff throw from Stewart and third on a ground out by Jackson Chourio. After an intentional walk of Turang, Contreras collected his third RBI of the game with a single to left field.
They did it again in the eighth against Edgardo Henriquez. Hamilton led off with a single, stole second and went to third on a ground out. Turang drove him in with an RBI single, giving the Brewers the first two-run lead for either team in this series. When Bauers drove in another run with a single, it gave the Brewers their first three-run lead this postseason.
Left to their own devices, the Dodgers couldn’t create another scoring opportunity. The final 15 batters went down in order against Brewers relievers Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby.
“They all throw 100 (mph) from different angles,” Freeman said.
The five perfect innings in relief are a postseason record. In winning the first two games of the NLCS, the Brewers’ bullpen has pitched 9⅔ scoreless innings.
“They attack hitters. They throw strikes. They’ve got good stuff, They throw hard,” Teoscar Hernandez said. “We just got to do a better job.
“I mean, they threw, the last two days, the same pitchers beside the starters. So we know what we’re gonna get during the games. They trust those guys. So that’s the guys that we’re gonna get.”
The Dodgers do not face elimination yet. But they must win two out of three at home in order to avoid it.
“We’ve got to find a way to get hits. That’s really it,” Betts repeated.
“They’re a really good ballclub. Really good arms. They’re swinging it. They’re playing really well. We have to come and be ready to go. There’s no secrets. We’re playing the game the same way. We’ve just got to find a way to get those hits.”

The Milwaukee Brewers set the series tone on Sunday night with a narrow victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 1 of the NLCS. Powered by excellent infield defense, which produced three ground-ball double plays, an incredible swing from Brice Turang that led to a game-tying home run off Tarik Skubal, and another dominant performance from their bullpen, Pat Murphy's squad built a key 1-0 series lead in their quest to knock off the reigning back-to-back World Series champs.
After Turang's game-tying solo shot in the fourth, the Brewers took the lead in the bottom of the fifth thanks to an RBI single from rookie right fielder Luis Lara. The Brewers maintained that narrow one-run lead through the final four innings of the series opener, but they certainly had opportunities to add on to their run total.
Milwaukee's best scoring opportunity came in the bottom of the eighth inning. Jackson Chourio led off the inning with a single to right field off right-handed reliever Evan Phillips. After the leadoff hit, Dodgers manager turned to southpaw Tanner Scott to face Brice Turang, who promptly laid down a sacrifice bunt to advance Chourio to second base, setting up an RBI opportunity for William Contreras.
However, with the left-handed Scott on the mound, Roberts elected to intentionally walk Contreras, setting up a tough left-on-left matchup for Jake Bauers. Scott struck out Bauers on six pitches, which brought lefty-crusher Andrew Vaughn to the plate. Once again, Roberts elected to intentionally walk the righty to set up a left-on-left matchup with Garrett Mitchell. In doing so, however, Roberts moved a key insurance run to third base, where a passed ball or wild pitch would have given the Brewers a two-run lead, and a single would have given them a three-run advantage.
It was undoubtedly a risk for Roberts and the Dodgers -- loading the bases for Mitchell -- but one that paid off on Sunday night. However, in doing so, Roberts exposed a strategy he may use throughout the remainder of the series: prioritizing matchups between his left-handed relievers and the Brewers' left-handed hitters. Such a strategy means the Brewers lefties will have to find ways to produce against Los Angeles' tough bullpen southpaws throughout the series.
The pressure is on the Brewers' left-handed hitters to produce against Dodgers' tough lefty relievers
Left-on-left matchups are something the Brewers are bound to see a lot of throughout the NLCS. From starters Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell to a quartet of lefty relievers in Alex Vesia, Tanner Scott, Kris Bubic, and Justin Wrobleski, Milwaukee can expect to see plenty of southpaws throughout their rematch with the Dodgers.
Clearly, based on last night's strategy, Roberts is going to prioritize matching those lefties up with the Brewers' left-handed hitters by any means necessary. That means there will likely be situations, like last night, where Bauers, Mitchell, Brice Turang, and Christian Yelich will be asked to produce against a same-side pitcher. Concerningly for the Brewers, of that group only Bauers (.901 OPS vs. LHP) had an OPS better than .668 against left-handed pitching during the regular season.
Bauers commented on his improved success against left-handed pitching this year during his pre-game press conference on Monday morning, saying, "A lot of it just has to do with getting the opportunity to see them more often, and then I think I've really focused on developing an approach that gives me the best chance."
On the topic of opportunities, Bauers set a new career-high with 160 plate appearances against left-handed pitchers this year, and already that practice against lefties is coming in handy in the NLCS. Bauers acknowledged the difficult southpaws on the Dodgers' NLCS roster, saying, "Some of these guys, obviously it's not easy, whether it be high arm slot coming from behind you or someone throwing from the side," but in four at-bats in Game 1 last night, all of which came against left-handed pitchers, Bauers went 1-for-3 with a walk and a hard-hit single. Pair that with Turang's impressive blast off Skubal, and the Brewers' left-handers are off to a strong start against same-side pitchers in the NLCS.
Assuming Roberts continues to prioritize these matchups, even if it means intentionally putting runners on base, the pressure will be on Bauers, Turang, and the rest of the Brewers' lefties to continue putting together strong at-bats in these situations. If they can find success against southpaws early in the series, it will certainly complicate Roberts' pitching plan going forward.

The New York Yankees need more dependable bullpen innings in 2027, and one possible answer is still pitching in October. Los Angeles Dodgers left-hander Alex Vesia deserves consideration as New York evaluates its offseason options.
Vesia appeared in NLCS Game 1 on October 11, when MLB highlighted his pickoff of Jake Bauers. His postseason role provides a timely opportunity to assess a pitcher who could strengthen the Yankees’ relief corps.
The connection remains an analysis of roster fit. The sources reviewed do not establish Yankees negotiations with Vesia, and New York has not announced an agreement.
However, his regular-season performance gives the idea substance. Vesia finished 2026 with a 2.64 ERA and 74 strikeouts in 58 innings, according to MLB’s statistics.
Alex Vesia Could Give the Yankees Another Late-Inning Option
That strikeout total translates to approximately 11.5 per nine innings. For a bullpen trying to escape jams without relying on its defense, the ability to miss bats offers a useful starting point.
Joe Najarian’s October 10 Yankees On SI assessment identified relief depth as an offseason concern. He also noted that Brent Headrick led MLB with 81 appearances.
That workload makes another dependable option valuable. A deeper group would give the manager more choices when Headrick needs rest or when an opponent presents a difficult stretch of hitters.
Vesia should be evaluated as a potential complement to Headrick. Adding another left-hander would make sense if he can handle the required matchups, rather than simply duplicate a role New York already fills.
The Yankees should also examine walk rate, performance against right-handed hitters and availability on consecutive days. A strong ERA does not answer every question about how a reliever fits.
That should include inherited runners. A reliever who strands traffic can offer different value from one whose best work starts with an empty inning.
The Yankees’ Closer Decision Still Comes First
David Bednar’s pending free agency creates a separate issue. Signing Vesia would not automatically resolve the ninth inning, and New York should avoid treating one successful addition as a complete bullpen rebuild.
The cleaner plan would address the closer job while strengthening the innings that lead to it. That could involve retaining Bednar and pursuing another experienced arm, depending on contract demands.
MLB lists Vesia among the upcoming free agents. His market could develop differently from New York’s preferred timetable, so the Yankees need alternatives rather than a plan tied to one pitcher.
Price matters, too. There is no verified contract forecast establishing that Vesia would be cheaper than other prominent relief options. His value to the Yankees should determine their offer, with room remaining for additional needs.
For now, the Dodgers’ postseason run gives New York another useful offseason name to evaluate. Vesia’s strikeouts make him an intriguing candidate, but the strongest argument is how he could distribute responsibility across the bullpen.
The Yankees need several trustworthy paths through the late innings. Vesia could help create one of them.

De cara a su tercera Serie de Campeonato consecutiva en la postemporada de las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB), los Dodgers tendrían una de las mejores noticias posibles para su relevo con el boricua Edwin Díaz de regreso en su mejor forma, lo que eventualmente le permitirá tomar la mayor cantidad de oportunidades como el cerrador del equipo que busca un tricampeonato en la Serie Mundial.
Sugar endulza el relevo de Dodgers para la SCLN
Díaz, que tuvo una tropezada temporada de debut con los Dodgers por una lesión en el codo y otra más en el cuello, tuvo números atípicos para uno de los mejores cerradores de los últimos años en las Grandes Ligas. De regreso en la Serie de Campeonato, el Sugar completó oportunidades de salvamento consecutivas en el Juego 3 y el Juego 4.
“Las últimas dos noches... esa es la razón por la que adquirimos a alguien como Edwin Díaz”, dijo Roberts después de que los Dodgers ganaran la Serie Divisional. “Es uno de los grandes cerradores del juego. Que esté lanzando a su mejor nivel justo ahora es lo que uno espera, y le doy mucho mérito por ello”.
Si bien Roberts y los Dodgers no ha designado nuevamente a Díaz como su cerrador nuevamente, sí le da una opción más para situaciones de alta exigencia con 8 juegos más por ganar para conquistar el tricampeonato del Clásico de Otoño.
“Creo que eso fue lo más importante para mí: que el equipo confía en mí”, dijo Díaz después del último juego de la SDLN. “Me dan la pelota todos los días... Por eso vine aquí, para ganar partidos y cerrar encuentros como este. Así que estoy muy contento en este momento”.
¿Qué opciones tiene Dodgers en el relevo?
Con Díaz volviendo a su nivel élite, los Dodgers pueden barajear las opciones en juegos de alta exigencia, especialmente con Tanner Scott (25 salvamentos en la temporada regular) y Evan Phillips (un rescate en la campaña).
Scott tiene tiempo para reponerse luego del golpe que puede representar recibir un jonrón de dos carreras en el Juego 1 de la Serie Divisional y después registrar holds –ventajas de 3 o menos carreras sostenidas en relevo intermedio– durante el octavo episodio del Juego 3 y 4. Phillips relevó a Scott para quedarse con el salvamento del Juego 1.
Esas dos opciones sirviendo como preparadores le permiten a los Dodgers jugar a Alex Vesia y Edgardo Henriquez como relevo intermedio; Vesia en duelos de zurdo contra zurdo y el venezolano Henriquez en diestro contra diestro.

- Click here to listen to this article
He pounded his chest twice as he left the batter’s box, and all of Dodgers nation rocked to the beat.
Andy Pages did it. He finally did it. He finally broke out of his baffling two-year October slump with a hit so powerful, he didn’t even have to climb over Kiké Hernández to get it.
How powerful? With one smooth swing he broke a tie by scoring two runs while sending two teams packing, the Atlanta Braves trudging home for the winter and the Dodgers charging into the National League Championship Series.
Yeah, it was a blast, both figuratively and literally, Pages’ two-out, two-strike bases-loaded single in the seventh inning Wednesday night silencing the lame tomahawk-chopping fans at Truist Park and giving the Dodgers an eventual clinching 4-1 victory against the Braves in the National League Division Series.
Certainly, it only gets tougher from here. In winning this best-of-five series three games to one, the Dodgers can now prepare for a best-of-seven showdown task against either the mighty Milwaukee Brewers or blazing San Diego Padres.
Yes, they will need to hit better, they will need Blake Snell to find his focus, they will need Shohei Ohtani to show up.
But…Andy Pages! Seriously! If a guy who was seven for 66 in the last two postseasons and was so helpless last year he was benched for the last three games of the World Series…if that guy can drive in the winning run from the bottom of the order? The once-fallible Dodgers may just be unbeatable.
“There’s no more talented team than the Los Angeles Dodgers,” manager Dave Roberts shouted in the postgame clubhouse. “We’re the best organization in sports, top to bottom. We’re smarter, we’re better, and we’re tougher.”
At that point, someone referenced a recent comment from Padres owner José E. Feliciano insinuating that the Dodgers, baseball’s oldest team, was composed of dinosaurs.
“And we’re dinosaurs!” shouted a voice above the clubhouse din.
If they’re dinosaurs, their first initial is “T” and their last name is ‘Rex.”
It’s OK to start seriously thinking about a three-peat now. They’re now just eight wins away but, given how mediocre the American League playoff teams appear, they could realistically be just four wins away.
Andy Pages comes through in the seventh inning to break a tie and four relievers close out a 3-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves to win the NLDS in four games.
Here’s guessing that the NLCS will be the real World Series. And here’s guessing the Dodgers will be ready.
Pages, who won the hearts of Dodger fans last October when he made a leaping game-saving catch over the back of Kiké Hernández, was granted his first big October swing thanks to the Braves largess.
In the seventh inning of a 1-all tie, Teoscar Hernández redeemed himself for another fielding blunder with a single that finally drove dizzying Tyler Mahle from the game.
In came Game 2 rookie sensation Didier Fuentes, only this time, he was all rookie and zero sensation, walking Josue De Paula and Kyle Tucker to load the bases. Considering De Paula is just a kid and Tucker has been struggling, the fact that both showed such patience in such a pressure situation was pretty cool. And moments later, it got even cooler.
In came veteran reliever Robert Suarez, and Pages was ready for him, working the count full before lining the two-run single up the middle.
The Dodgers added a run two innings later on a Max Muncy home run — has there ever been a playoff game when he hasn’t homered? — to finalize the score.
When the game ended on an Austin Riley fly out to right field, Pages celebrated in center field by taking off his cap, turning his face to the sky and pounding the cap three times into his glove.
It was a series that was worth the emotion, the Dodgers famous starting rotation giving up just four runs in 21 ⅓ innings, the bullpen solid behind a revived Edwin Díaz, and the offense doing just enough to beat Braves aces Chris Sale and Mahle.
In the fifth inning of a tie game, starter Tyler Glasnow issued walks to Riley and Michael Harris II. With two out, in came Alex Vesia. Up stepped slugger Matt Olson. The fans climbed to their feet. This was the Braves’ big chance.
But Olson swung at the first pitch and lined it directly to second baseman Kiké Hernández to end the threat and quiet the joint. Díaz threw a hitless ninth for his second save of the series and…who’s going to beat them?
Afterward, Roberts referenced nearly half of his team when talking about his pride. He talked about Pages’ hit, about De Paula’s walk, about reliever Edgardo Henriquez’s 1 ⅔ shutout innings, about Muncy’s bat and Freddie Freeman’s glove
“I guess, amazement,” he said. “Our guys just continue to fight, persevere. You never know who the guy’s going to be.”
The only glaring weakness was, once again, the superstar who used to be their strength. Ohtani scored the Dodgers’ first run after drawing a walk but went hitless in three ensuing at-bats. He only got two hits in the four-game series and you have to wonder if his injury-wracked body would be better out of the lineup.
How well are they playing without the full services of their most historic player? On the verge of making history, the Dodgers don’t even miss him.

8 de octubre de 2026 - 9:55 PM
Atlanta - Andy Pages impulsó dos carreras con un sencillo con las bases llenas en la séptima entrada para darle la ventaja definitiva a Los Ángeles, y los reinante bicampeones Dodgers vencieron el miércoles 4-1 a los Braves de Atlanta para sentenciar su serie divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Los Dodgers ganaron juegos consecutivos en Atlanta para llevarse 3-1 la serie al mejor de cinco y avanzar a la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional dentro de empeño por convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional que conquista tres Series Mundiales seguidas.
El cubano Pages conectó una línea por el centro a un lanzamiento en cuenta de 3-2 del venezolano Robert Suárez para remolcar al dominicano Teoscar Hernández, quien había empalmado un sencillo ante el abridor Tyler Mahle, y al corredor emergente Tommy Edman, para poner el 3-1 en el marcador 3-1.
Acto seguido, el colombiano Didier Fuentes concedió base por bolas al bateador emergente dominicano Josue De Paula y a Kyle Tucker para congestionar las bases. Edman corrió por De Paula.
El jonrón solitario de Max Muncy ante el cubano Raisel Iglesias en la novena aumentó la ventaja y dejó al toletero con un gran total de 19 cuadrangulares de postemporada con los Dodgers, ampliando su récord de la franquicia.
El derecho de los Dodgers Tyler Glasnow, en su primera apertura desde el 24 de septiembre, permitió apenas un hit, pero otorgó cinco bases por bolas en cuatro innings y dos tercios.
Después de conceder dos boletos en la quinta, el zurdo Alex Vesia terminó la entrada con un rodado de Matt Olson a la segunda base.
La oportunidad desperdiciada dejó a los Braves con 18 pasaporte en la serie, pero ninguno se concretó en carrera.
Glasnow y cuatro relevistas se combinaron para permitir apenas tres hits. Tanner Scott lanzó una octava entrada perfecta antes de que el puertorriqueño Edwin “Sugar” Díaz sacara tres outs rápidos para apuntarse el salvamento.
Fue el segundo salvamento en noches consecutivas para Díaz, de vuelta en el puesto de cerrador de los Dodgers.
Mahle, originario de Newport Beach, California, y que creció como aficionado de los Dodgers, permitió dos carreras —una limpia— en seis innings y un tercio.
Michael Harris II conectó el primer lanzamiento de Glasnow para un sencillo antes de robarse la segunda y, finalmente, anotar desde tercera con un lanzamiento descontrolado que rebotó en el protector de pecho del receptor Will Smith.
Los Dodgers empataron en la segunda con ayuda de dos errores de Atlanta. Shohei Ohtani recibió base por bolas, se robó la segunda y avanzó a tercera por un tiro desviado del receptor Sean Murphy hacia el jardín central. El elevado de Muncy a la zona corta del jardín izquierdo fue dejado caer por el campocorto hondureño Mauricio Dubón para otro error, lo que permitió que Ohtani anotara.
Hernández se estrelló contra la pared al intentar atrapar el doble de Ozzie Albies ante Vesia para abrir la sexta. Hernández se señaló la cabeza y el cuello al hablar con un preparador físico, pero se mantuvo en el juego.
El venezolano Edgardo Henríquez dejó varado a Albies en segunda. Henríquez permitió un hit al cubrir una entrada y dos tercios sin carrera para llevarse la victoria.
Las noticias explicadas de forma sencilla y directa para entender lo más importante del día.

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — Dave Roberts didn’t hesitate.
So what if Tyler Glasnow had thrown only 78 pitches?
So what if he was still in the fifth inning?
Glasnow had walked his second batter of the inning, and Roberts wasn’t about to take any chances.
Calling on Alex Vesia to record the final out of the inning, Roberts initiated a chaotic sequence of events that resulted in the Dodgers claiming a 4-1 victory over the Braves in Game 4 of their National League Division Series.
The Dodgers advanced to the NL Championship Series.
Because of Tarik Skubal.
Because of Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
Because of Freddie Freeman.
And because of David Ray Roberts, the manager affectionately known as Doc who has a game or two like this every October.
The victory over the Braves on Wednesday was a Doctober classic.
On a day in which one of his four aces lasted only 4 ⅔ innings, Roberts figured out how to cover 13 outs of the game with a notoriously unpredictable bullpen.
Roberts’ fingerprints were also all over Andy Pages’ two-run single in the seventh inning that broke open the game.
When Teoscar Hernandez singled that inning with one out, Braves manager Walt Weiss replaced starting pitcher Tyler Mahle with right-hander Didier Fuentes.
Fuentes forced Max Muncy to ground out, but Hernandez advanced to second base on the play.
Due up was Game 3 hero Kike Hernandez.
Rather than have the right-handed utilityman face Fuentes, Roberts deployed rookie Josue De Paula as a pinch hitter. The left-handed-hitting De Paula drew a walk, at which point he was replaced on the basepaths by Tommy Edman.
Kyle Tucker followed up with another walk to load the bases, at which point Weiss turned to fireballer Robert Suarez to pitch to Pages.
Pages batted .078 in the postseason last year, which resulted in his benching in the World Series. He was 0-for-7 in the first two games of this series, but Roberts stuck with him.
Roberts’ faith was rewarded by the most important hit of Pages’ three-year career, a single to right field that drove in two runs to push the Dodgers in front, 3-1. The runs were the Dodgers’ first of the series that weren’t scored via a home run.
The manager demonstrated an equal level of creativity in directing his bullpen.
Vesia returned for the sixth inning, only to give up a leadoff double to Ozzie Albies. Roberts kept the left-hander in for another batter, the left-handed-hitting Drake Baldwin, who lined out.
Roberts’ next call to the bullpen was for Edgardo Henriquez, who spent the last two weeks of the regular season on the injured list. Henriquez gave up a run in the Dodgers’ Game 2 loss, but not only did Roberts trust him to prevent Albies from scoring, he also had him pitch the seventh inning.
From there, it was simple.
Tanner Scott pitched the eighth inning. With Muncy homering in the ninth inning to increase the lead to 4-1, Edwin Diaz came in to record the last three outs.
The Dodgers moved to within four wins of playing in their third consecutive World Series, and they did it with Shohei Ohtani still missing in action.
Ohtani was 2-for-13 in this series.
“It’s good to know that we can still win games without him doing a whole bunch,” Roberts said. “But he’s going to come to life. It will happen.”
Roberts has squinted extra hard in recent days to find evidence of that.
Here’s the reality: In his last 22 combined games between the regular season and playoffs, Ohtani has no home runs and only one RBI.
That isn’t a slump.
The No. 1 player in the game doesn’t go this long without hitting in the prime of his career without something being seriously wrong with him.
Ohtani spent 15 days last month on the injured list because of a discomfort in his right arm. A couple of days before he was placed on the IL, he said his left knee was also bothering him.
The uncertainty over Ohtani’s capabilities forced Roberts to move him around the lineup.
With Mookie Betts grinding out quality at-bats as the leadoff hitter and Freeman producing enough to solidify his place as the team’s No. 2 hitter, Ohtani was removed from the top of the order.
Against the left-handed Chris Sale in Game 3, Ohtani batted fifth. Against the right-handed Mahle on Wednesday, he batted cleanup.
Ohtani managed to create something out of nothing in the second inning. He drew a walk, then stole second base, prompting Braves catcher Sean Murphy to airmail a throw into center field. Ohtani scampered to third base. When Braves shortstop Mauricio Dubón dropped a popup by Muncy in shallow left field, Ohtani scored to tie the game at 1.
Ohtani didn’t collect any hits Wednesday, but he didn’t have to.
Roberts had the game under control.

ATLANTA — Andy Pages’ two-run single in the seventh inning broke open a pitchers’ duel and helped the Los Angeles Dodgers close out their National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves with a 4-1 win in Game 4 on Wednesday.
The Dodgers, who won the series 3-1 and are looking to be the first National League team to win three straight World Series, await the winner of the other NLDS between the Brewers and Padres. Milwaukee leads that best-of-five set 2-1 entering a Wednesday matchup in San Diego.
Pages’ hit was Los Angeles’ first with runners in scoring position in the series after the team started 0-for-14. It came off of Robert Suarez after Teoscar Hernandez hit a one-out single against Braves starter Tyler Mahle and then reliever Didier Fuentes issued back-to-back two-out walks.
Pages had two of the Dodgers’ five hits and two of their three RBIs in the win.
His clutch hit came the inning after Atlanta got nothing out of Ozzie Albies’ leadoff double, with Edgardo Henriquez (1-0) escaping the jam to earn his first career postseason victory.
Los Angeles’ Max Muncy tacked on an insurance run with a solo homer in the ninth, his third long ball of the postseason.
Mahle (0-1) was a tough-luck loser, charged with two runs (one earned) on three hits over 6 1/3 innings. He struck out four and walked one.
Michael Harris II had two of Atlanta’s three hits, including a double. However, the Braves’ situational hitting issues continued as they finished the series 1-for-23 with runners in scoring position.
Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow battled through 4 1/3 innings, allowing just one run on one hit, walking five and striking out five. Alex Vesia, Henriquez, Tanner Scott and Edwin Diaz followed and combined to allow no runs on two hits over the final 4 1/3 innings, setting down the final seven Atlanta batters in a row.
Diaz earned his second save of the series.
Los Angeles’ pitching staff gave up eight runs on 18 hits over the four-game series.
The Braves opened the scoring in the bottom of the first on a wild pitch that scored Harris. He led off with a single, stole second and moved to third on a fielder’s choice.
The Dodgers equalized in the second behind a pair of Braves errors. Shohei Ohtani drew a leadoff walk, stole second and moved to third on an errant throw from catcher Sean Murphy. Muncy then hit a sky-high popup to shallow left that shortstop Mauricio Dubon dropped, allowing Ohtani to score.
–Curt Weiler, Field Level Media
