ATLANTA — Overmatched last postseason and benched during the World Series, Andy Pages used the embarrassment to fuel an All-Star season in 2026.
But he was hit by a pitch on Aug. 21 that broke a bone in his hand, didn’t return until the final six games of the regular season and started the postseason, trying to do too much (by his manager’s estimation) to make up for last fall’s lack of contributions.
The accounts have been reconciled. It was Pages’ clutch two-out, two-run single in the seventh inning that broke a tie and lifted the Dodgers to a 4-1 victory on Wednesday night in Game 4 of their National League Division Series with the Atlanta Braves.
The victory sends the Dodgers to the National League Championship Series against either the Milwaukee Brewers or San Diego Padres. The Dodgers have reached baseball’s Final Four for the fifth time in the past seven years, the eighth time in the past 11. Their quest for a ‘three-peat’ will continue Sunday either in Milwaukee or at home against the Padres.
This series was decided in the seventh inning.
With the score tied 1-1, Teoscar Hernandez – fresh off a collision with the left field wall that left him on the warning track dirt, rubbing the left side of his head – singled with one out off Braves starter Tyler Mahle. It was just the third hit off Mahle and it came on just his 85th pitch. But Braves manager Walt Weiss went to his bullpen, bringing in Game 2 hero Didier Fuentes to face Max Muncy.
Fuentes got Muncy to ground out, Hernandez moving to second, but he walked pinch-hitter Josue De Paula and Kyle Tucker to load the bases with two outs.
Weiss had a quick hook, pulling Fuentes and handing the ball to veteran Robert Suarez to face Pages. Pages got ahead in the count, 3-and-1, then swung and missed at a 99.1 mph fastball from Suarez. He got another fastball on the full count and didn’t miss, stroking it through the middle for the Dodgers’ first – and only hit – with a runner in scoring position in their 16 at-bats in those situations during the four games of this series.
Runs had been hard to come by in Atlanta. After Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Chris Sale squared off in Game 3, Mahle and Tyler Glasnow allowed just a dirty run each through the first six innings.
In the bottom of the first, Michael Harris II led off with a single off of Glasnow. He stole second, went to third on a ground out and score when Glasnow spiked a knuckle curve in the dirt well in front of home plate. It bounced off Will Smith’s chest protector back towards the mound and Glasnow couldn’t retrieve it in time to get Harris.
In the top of the second, Shohei Ohtani took a five-pitch walk, stole second and went to third when Braves catcher Sean Murphy threw the ball into center field. Ohtani scored when Braves shortstop Mauricio Dubon dropped Max Muncy’s pop-up in shallow left field.
Mahle struck out only four in his 6⅓ innings (three of them consecutively in the fourth inning) and got just seven swings-and-misses on 95 pitches. But he got a lot of soft contact – and when he didn’t, it usually found a Braves fielder’s glove. The Dodgers hit seven balls in the first six innings with exit velocities of 95 mph or higher (the StatCast standard for “hard-hit”). Only one of them was a base hit – Pages’ third-inning single (106.7 mph).
Against Glasnow, the Braves just didn’t make much contact at all.
He gave up that leadoff single to Harris in the first inning but no other hits. He did walk five, though, including two in the fifth inning that prompted Manager Dave Roberts to pull him from the game after 78 pitches.
Dodgers pitchers somehow walked 18 batters in the series but let none of them score. Alex Vesia retired Matt Olson to end that fifth inning. Edgardo Henriquez held the Braves scoreless over the next two. Tanner Scott retired the slumping heart of the Braves’ order and Muncy gave Edwin Diaz cushion in the ninth inning with a solo home run (his 19th career postseason homer, a franchise record).
More to come on this story.

Tyler Glasnow had some choice words after being pulled from Game 4 of the NLDS on Wednesday.
Glasnow got the start on Wednesday for the Los Angeles Dodgers in their potential closeout game against the Atlanta Braves. He ended up going 4.2 innings, allowing just one hit and one earned run but also walking five total batters.
With two outs in the fifth inning at Truist Park in Atlanta, Ga., Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made the decision to pull Glasnow. The righty Glasnow had just walked his second batter of the inning to put the Dodgers in a precarious position with the score tied 1-1.
As Roberts came out to get him, Glasnow was shown cursing on the FOX Sports broadcast. He appeared to say, “That’s f–king crazy.” Here is the video (but obviously watch out for the bad language).
As of now the Dodgers have issued 18 walks in this series and not a single one has scored. Glasnow issued 5 in his 4.2 innings & was NOT happy about the early hook. https://t.co/bI8Bnlzm5O
— Dallas Braden (@DALLASBRADEN209) October 7, 2026
Glasnow was only at 78 pitches at the time that he was pulled. But as evidenced by the five walks, he did not quite have his best stuff during Wednesday’s game.
Dodgers reliever Alex Vesia came into the contest for Glasnow and ultimately secured the final out, getting Braves slugger Matt Olson to ground out. While Roberts has been criticized many times in the past for seemingly overmanaging his pitching staff, he certainly appeared to have made the right call there.

It took until the seventh inning of the fourth game of the National League Division Series for the Dodgers to get their first hit with a runner in scoring position. But Andy Pages made it count, with a two-run single to break a tie in a 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves on Wednesday night at Truist Park, clinching the NLCS to send the Dodgers to their third National League Championship Series in a row.
The winning rally started with a single by Teoscar Hernández, just minutes after crashing into the left field wall on a Braves double in the previous half-inning. That ended the night for Tyler Mahle, who continued to have the Dodgers number, once again pitching into the seventh.
In came Game 2 Braves hero Didier Fuentes, whose second batter faced was fellow 21-year-old pinch-hitter Josue De Paula, only 24 days his senior. De Paula, in just his second postseason plate appearance, walked, then was removed for pinch-runner Tommy Edman. Kyle Tucker also walked to load the bases, setting up Pages — the Dodgers RBI leader this season — to single home a pair.
After going hitless in his first two games this series, Pages had two hits in Game 3 and two more in Game 4, equaling his total for the entire postseason in 2025. The hit also snapped an 0-for-14 skid by the Dodgers with runners in scoring position to start this series.
The first of those runs snapped a string of 22 straight innings by Mahle against the Dodgers without allowing an earned run, dating all the way back to 2022.
Edgardo Henriquez, who entered with one out in the sixth inning and stranded a runner on second, followed with a scoreless seventh inning to bookend the Dodgers rally, and earned the win.
Just like in Game 3, Tanner Scott pitched a scoreless eighth and Edwin Díaz closed out the win in the ninth, giving the Dodgers the planned back end of their bullpen that hadn't really been fully intact since early April.
Dodgers pitchers allowed eight total runs in the four-game series.
Max power
Max Muncy added some insurance with a solo home run in the ninth inning, extending his Dodgers career postseason record with now 19 home runs. Muncy also homered in Games 1 and 2 of this series, matching his most prolific postseason series with the long ball. He also hit three home runs in the 2019 NLDS against the Washington Nationals.
Sloppy start
Both teams exchanged mistakes for each other's first run, including an errant throw into center field on a stolen base attempt from each side. Michael Harris II got a great jump from third base on a wild pitch by Tyler Glasnow that didn't get too far from home plate in the first inning, catching the Dodgers flat-footed. In the top of the second, Shohei Ohtani walked, stole second and went to third on the bad throw, then scored when a Max Muncy popup into short left field was biffed by shortstop Mauricio Dubón.
Glasnow improved a bit as the game progressed, and didn't allow another hit after Harris led off the game with a single. But, like Blake Snell in Game 2, Glasnow on Wednesday walked five batters, including two in the fifth inning — a leadoff free pass to Austin Riley after getting ahead 0-2, and a two-out, four-pitch walk to Ronald Acuña Jr. to end Glasnow's night early.
The Dodgers right-hander struck out five with those five walks in his 4 2/3 innings, and like Snell limited the damage to only one run. Alex Vesia helped, inducing a groundout to second base to end the fifth inning with those two Glasnow walks left stranded on base, and the game still tied.
Glasnow threw 78 pitches, 44 for strikes.
Not so free passes
None of Glasnow's five walks in Game 4 scored, and none of the 18 Braves who walked in the NLDS have touched home plate. But there have still been costs to that Dodgers wildness. For one, the Dodgers had to turn to its bullpen much earlier than hoped in two of the four games.
Also, two of Snell's walks in the first inning of Game 2, pushing Acuña to third base, which allowed him to score on an infield single. In Game 3, the pinch-hit walk by Rowdy Tellez pushed Dubón to third base, which allowed him to score on a groundout. So the walks have been costly, even if not as much as perhaps they should have been.
NLDS Game 4 particulars
Home run: Max Muncy (3)
WP — Edgardo Henriquez (1-0): 1 2/3 IP, 1 hit
LP — Tyler Mahle (0-1): 6 1/3 IP, 3 hits, 2 runs (1 earned), 1 walk, 4 strikeouts
Sv — Edwin Díaz (2): 1 IP, 1 strikeout
Up next
The Dodgers move on to a third consecutive National League Championship Series, and eighth in the last 11 years, beginning Sunday night (time TBD, Fox Sports) either in Milwaukee against the Brewers or at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles against the Padres.

Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts ruled pitcher Blake Treinen out for the postseason after the right-hander suffered a shoulder injury warming up for a relief appearance in San Francisco.
Now, it sounds as if Roberts spoke prematurely.
Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said Saturday that Treinen's status for the postseason is "not decided firmly."
"It was clear for this round," Friedman said, "but we'll keep monitoring it as we go."
Friedman described the injury as "soreness" — a vague if much less ominous problem than the one Roberts suggested when Treinen was placed on the injured list after the Dodgers' Sept. 26 game against the Giants.
“I don't know if it was a complete blowout, but really unfortunate,” Roberts said at the time.
In 12 MLB seasons — the last six with the Dodgers — Treinen is 49-42 with a 2.94 ERA and 83 saves. Although he served as the Dodgers' closer only occasionally, he was a reliable source of strikeouts, low ERAs and some big postseason moments as the Dodgers captured three World Series championships this decade.
In 2024, Treinen saved three postseason games in three opportunities, allowing only three runs across nine October appearances. He was the winning pitcher in Game 5 of the 2024 World Series, when he threw 2.1 scoreless relief innings against the New York Yankees.
If the Dodgers need Treinen this month, it won't merely mean that he is healthy. It will mean somebody else — likely a couple somebodies — are not.
The Dodgers have enough quality and capable bullpen arms that they did not roster two pitchers who figured to be October mainstays (left-handers Justin Wrobleski and Jack Dreyer) in the National League Division Series. That decision was made in large part due to the Dodgers' opponent.
For Treinen to appear in a game this month, he'd have to prove more worthy of a roster spot than Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Brock Stewart, Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, Edgardo Henriquez, Edwin Diaz and Kris Bubic — plus Wrobleski and Dreyer.
Right-handers Bobby Miller and Emmet Sheehan have lockers and figure to be ready if called upon, too. Right-hander Will Klein finished the season on the injured list, like Treinen, but his throwing progression has put him in position to rejoin the roster if needed.
Treinen's possible availability is likely a mere footnote to the Dodgers' 2026 postseason run. Considering it sounded impossible a week ago, it's at least worth noting.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—Tomorrow marks the start of the Los Angeles Dodgers’ quest for a third consecutive World Series championship, beginning with a rematch against the Atlanta Braves in the 2026 National League Division Series.
Today, both clubs hold their final workout before Saturday’s scorching mid-day opener, and we’ve got plenty of new updates and clarity on the Dodgers’ plans for the two games this weekend.
Dodgers’ NLDS Rotation Comes Into Focus With Skubal Tabbed for Game One
Leading up to the postseason, many asked what order the Dodgers would put on their star-studded starting rotation, and now we have part of an answer: two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal will start Game One of the NLDS against the Braves on Saturday.
That was a shock to many, especially since 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto was considered the clear-cut favorite to lead the charge in the postseason.
The move also isn’t entirely based on the Braves’ struggles versus left-handed pitching this season; Skubal on Friday confirmed that he learned of his Game One start way back during his last outing in San Francisco, where he tossed seven shutout innings to close his 2026 regular season.
While Dave Roberts was less revealing about his outlook for Games Two and Three of the NLDS, he admitted the team would have a decision by the end of Friday’s workout, but the stars are starting to align themselves on what the likely order will be.
Yamamoto, who faced hitters on Wednesday, is now lined up to start on regular rest against the Braves during Game Three, as reported by Taro Abe of Japan’s Chunichi Sports.
That would place left-hander Blake Snell for Game Two, after Skubal and before Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow, who threw a simulated game on Thursday for a possible Game Four if needed.
There were really no “wrong” answers for Dave Roberts and the Dodgers, but this allows them to focus on the Braves’ left-handed disadvantage and decide whether to go for the series sweep or swing with their best starter, Yamamoto, on the mound in Game Three, where he’ll likely go toe-to-toe with Chris Sale.
Dodgers Look to Exploit Braves’ Left-Handed Weakness With Southpaw-Heavy Staff
After tabbed left-hander Tarik Skubal with the ball in Game One of the NLDS, it starts a running theme for the Dodgers’ plan against the Braves, and that is their inability and struggles to hit left-handed pitching.
The Braves posted just a 91 wRC+ against southpaws during the regular season, tied for 24th in MLB. They also ranked 21st in wOBA (.306), 28th in OBP (.300), and tied for 16th in batting average (.240), while their 7.0% walk rate against lefties ranked 29th.
That combination gives the Dodgers plenty of reason to load up on southpaws in the NLDS, particularly with Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell available. Skubal is already set to start Game One, giving Los Angeles a lefty right out of the gate.
Atlanta’s overall offense was productive enough to win 94 games, but its struggles against lefties provide the Dodgers with a specific weakness to attack throughout the series.
While the Dodgers have yet to announce a Game Two starter, all signs point to fellow left-hander Blake Snell, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto to follow him in Game Three at Atlanta.
As far as the Dodgers’ bullpen construction, depending on what split they have on the 26-man roster, they have plenty of left-handed options to choose from, including deadline acquisition Kris Bubic.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts confirmed Friday that the team would go with a 14-12 split for their 26-man roster, and with four starting pitchers, that leaves eight spots for the bullpen, with left-handers Tanner Scott, Jack Dreyer and Alex Vesia locked for that role.
Chris Sale Likely Out of Games One and Two as Dodgers Avoid Atlanta’s Ace Early
In an effort to push the Braves past the Phillies for their first postseason series win since the 2021 season, Chris Sale came in on two days of rest out of the bullpen to collect the final four outs of Game Three.
Despite the Braves leading 6-2 and their closer, Raisel Iglesias, available in the bullpen, new Braves skipper Walt Weiss opted for the kill shot by bringing in his best pitcher, Chris Sale.
That move, however important it was for that particular game, has changed the landscape of the Braves’ pitching plan for the NLDS, as Sale is not lined up to pitch Game One and now may not be in play for Game Two on Sunday either.
“We’re gonna err on the side of giving him (time to rest) if it’s even close… A lot of it’s going to depend on how Chris feels… Certainly don’t want to jeopardize him and his health. He just happened to feel great yesterday when he got to the park, and that’s why he was in play.”
While this could simply be Walt Weiss playing a little October gamesmanship, keeping Chris Sale away from Games One and Two would certainly give Atlanta a chance to catch the Dodgers off guard, though Dave Roberts has plenty of postseason experience himself.
Of course, Weiss could also be telling the truth. If Atlanta really plans to save Sale for his return to Truist Park, the Braves’ decision to use him in relief during Game Three of the Wild Card Series becomes even more curious.
The Braves are already down two starters in left-hander Martín Pérez and right-hander Bryce Elder, with Weiss confirming that both will not be on the NLDS roster but possibly on the NLCS roster if Atlanta advances.
That leaves the Braves with a trio of Chris Sale (down until Game Three), Tyler Mahle, and Grant Holmes, who has been used in relief as a bulk inning guy from the bullpen.
The Braves are likely to launch a bullpen game for Game One in Los Angeles on Saturday, with Mahle set to start Game Two on normal rest after a masterful outing tossing seven innings of one-run ball.
Still, the likelihood of the Dodgers seeing Sale only once this series, and as late as Game Three, is a massive advantage for Dave Roberts and Co.
Dodgers vs. Braves: How the 2026 Head-to-Head Series Shook Out
The Dodgers didn’t exactly dominate their head-to-head matchup with the Braves this season. Los Angeles went just 1-5 against Atlanta in six regular-season meetings, getting outscored 26-15 in the process.
The teams first met at Dodger Stadium from May 8th-10th, with the Dodgers taking the opener 3-1 before Atlanta won the next two games by identical 7-2 scores. The Braves then delivered an even bigger blow in the final regular-season series, sweeping Los Angeles at Truist Park from August 25th-27th. Atlanta won the opener by one run, walked off in the middle game, and finished the sweep with a 1-0 Chris Sale shutout.
This matchup also comes with some unfinished postseason business. The Dodgers and Braves last met in the 2021 NLCS, when Atlanta knocked Los Angeles out in six games before winning the World Series. The Dodgers battled back from a 2-0 series deficit to cut the deficit to one game, but the Braves slammed the door in Game Six at Truist Park.
Five years later, the two teams meet again with another trip to the NLCS on the line. After Atlanta owned the regular-season matchup, the Dodgers now have a chance to change the story when the NLDS opens Saturday at Dodger Stadium.

Whenever the Los Angeles Dodgers playoff journey ends, they'll need to make several decisions on how to fortifiy the bullpen. Much like playoff time last season, the unit has become a house of cards that feels as if it's on the verge of collapse, even if there's been good news recently.
One player who won't be part of the postseason bullpen is veteran right-hander Blake Treinen. He suffered a shoulder injury while warming up in the bullpen during September 26's matchup against the San Francisco Giants. The full extent isn't yet known, but it is significant enough for the Dodgers to announce that the 38-year-old is done for the year.
Treinen is a free-agent-to-be, and that sets the scene for Los Angeles to make a decision. Does the club let the long-time high-leverage hurler walk? Or does the team follow the route it took with Evan Phillips, whom they re-signed while he was recovering from Tommy John surgery, with hopes that he could return as an impact bullpen arm down the stretch?
It's time for the Dodgers to thank Blake Treinen for his service and let him ride off into the sunset
Listening to some of his peers talk about the injury, it's clear that Treinen is a well-liked and influential player within the Dodgers' bullpen.
“It’s gut-wrenching for us,” Alex Vesia said, via Jack Harris of the California Post. “Blake’s one of our leaders out there in the bullpen.”
We're not going to say that veteran leadership doesn't matter, but there are a few key differences between Treinen's situation and the circumstances surrounding Phillips at the time that LA decided to bring him back.
The first has to do with age. Phillips is six years younger, and that matters. If Treinen were to come back and try to pitch in 2027, it would be for his age-39 season, making it extremely questionable as to whether or not he'd have anything left in the tank.
Timing matters too. As we saw with Phillips this year, it can take a bit for an injured reliever to get back into the groove. The 32-year-old was horrendous when he came back in July, throwing 7⅓ innings and surrendering five earned runs, including four home runs, before settling in to post a 2.41 over his final 18⅔ innings from August 1 onward. Even then, he didn't fully hit his stride until September.
The injuries these two relievers have suffered are different, but the thought remains the same. Treinen was also up and down this year, posting a decent 3.64 ERA, which means he might not have that extra gear that Phillips does.
The most important difference, however, is that Phillips had been mostly healthy before his UCL injury, whereas Treinen has dealt with a variety of maladies in recent years. He was limited to just 29⅔ innings this season and missed nearly two months with elbow inflammation. He dealt with forearm soreness in 2025 that limited him to just 26⅔ innings, dealt with a hip issue in 2024, and missed the entire 2023 campaign after undergoing shoulder surgery to repair his labrum and rotator cuff.
In fact, Treinen hasn't had a fully healthy year since 2021, so while he's put together dominant campaigns in the past, it's hard to expect him to be that same pitcher and avoid other injuries moving forward.
This should also be a lesson for the Dodgers, who have spent big on veteran relievers only to get mediocre results and a bunch of injuries. Relievers are volatile, and we saw that from Tanner Scott last year. We saw how quickly they can run out of gas with the Kirby Yates experiment. We're in the throes of it right now with Edwin Diaz.
The lesson from Phillips should be clear. Los Angeles originally acquired him off waivers from the Tampa Bay Rays in 2021. The Dodgers got him as a young player and made him into what he is today through their coaching and development plan. They need more of that and less star chasing in the pen, because the latter is more often than not a disappointment.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — With the end of the regular season on Sunday, the statisticians can finally put down their pencils. We had a near miss for the triple crown in the American League (Yordan Alvarez) and a pitcher with a sub-2.00 ERA in the National League (Jacob Misiorowski). And though no Dodgers were at the top of any statistically categories this year, there were plenty featured in the NL Top Ten. Let’s do a quick end-of-season rundown, shall we?
The plan for two-way dominance Cy Young/MVP consideration sort of flamed out before the All-Star break, and Shohei was struggling to find his footing at the plate in the aftermath of a couple of injuries (most notably his right knee). However, even a diminished Ohtani is among the league’s elite and Shohei did enough in the first half of the season to lock down some Top-Ten finishes. He was tied for ninth in home runs with 30, tied for tenth in walks with 81, and 19th in batting average with .275. His other numbers were also top-ten-worthy: he finished sixth in the NL in On-Base Percentage with .377 and fifth in slugging percentage with .512. And, finally, his OPS of .889 was more than 100 lower than last year, but still third in the league behind Chicago’s Pete Crow-Armstrong and the Nationals’ James Wood.
It was good year. But considering the wow factor of the first two years, a bit of a disappointment. Hopefully, he can get right in time to do damage like the old Shohei in the playoffs.
Despite his mighty struggles in September, Freddie turned in another strong campaign in 2026. Although his power number were down considerably, he still found his way on base at a clip not often seen in the modern game. Though his .288 batting average represented a low in Freddie’s Dodger years, it was still good enough for tenth place in the league. And, his 167 hits put him in eighth place in that category.
For those of you keeping track, he now stands at 2,598 hits in his career, 402 shy of the 3,000 mark that he’s had on his mind for a while. He’ll probably need three more years in the big league to reach that plateau, so that means the Dodgers would have to re-sign him after his current contract expires at the end of next year. Will that happen? It should, but I don’t know if Andrew Friedman wants to be sentimental about such things.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto was the only Dodger pitcher who logged enough innings to qualify for postseason awards, and he’s sure to get at least a sniff or two in the Cy Young voting. His year was probably his best yet: Fifth in wins (14), 3rd in ERA (2.53), 4th in innings pitched (185), 10th in strikeouts (182), 2nd in WHIP, and 2nd in Average Against (.182). Of course, all the hardwares going to the Miz this year, but Yamamoto’s steadiness is something to behold even if he doesn’t light up the radar gun on every pitch.
After a horrible year in 2025, no one was quite sure what to expect from Tanner Scott in 2026, and when Edwin Diaz went out with injury, there were more than a few Dodger fans who dreaded the thought of last year’s goat closing out games. However, Scott proved more than up to the task, converting 25 of 29 save opportunities, which put him in sixth place in the NL leader board. It will be interesting to see what happens as a resurgent Edwin Diaz seems to be ready for a return to the closer’s role.
Honorable mention….
Though they didn’t make any top tens, we should give it for Max Muncy, who made the All-Star team and finished 13th in the league in OPS and tied for 14th in the NL for homers. A really solid season from Max. Alex Vesia finished 7th in the league in appearances, and had an impact on more games than you might think. And, though they’re nowhere on the leaderboard, the strong finishes for Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez, and Kyle Tucker gives one hope for the postseason.
What about the team?
Since the Dodgers won the second most games in baseball, it only figures that they’d have a lot of nice numbers at the end of the year. On the hitting side, they finished fourth in home runs (204), fourth in RBI (756), 3rd in batting average (.257), second in slugging percentage (.424), and second in OPS (.762).
On the pitching side, they finished second in team ERA (3.55), 3rd in strikeouts (1,521), first in WHIP (1.18), and first in average against (.218). When you isolate the starters, the numbers are even better: first place in ERA, WHIP, and average against, and second in strikeouts.
The bullpen was good, but closer to the middle of the pack in the NL: fourth in ERA, fourth in saves, and fourth in WHIP. One stat that may work in the pen’s favor though: they finished 14th out of 15 NL teams in bullpen innings pitched. That means that other pens (save the Phillies) have been taxed more than the Dodgers. That could make a difference the deeper we go into October.
Conclusion
The numbers show kind of how 2026 felt: it was a good year, but not a dominant year. Many players, while still contributing, were down from their historical norms. And if the past is prologue, look for a lot of low-scoring games this October. Games that might be decided by one swing of the bat or one shut-down inning.
In the meantime, we wait. We watch and we wait.
See you Saturday!

item.content:encoded:
Now that the 2026 MLB regular season is done, Sony made one last ratings tweak for many of the players across the league on October 2. The October MLB The Show 26 ratings update saw Mookie Betts & Cade Smith rise to join the other Diamonds in the game.
The notable changes
Mookie Betts is back as a Diamond in MLB The Show 26. He and Cade Smith were the only two to move to Diamond status on October 2. Betts moved to 85 OVR after a strong final few weeks. Over his last 14 games, Betts slashed .316/.418/.632 with four home runs and 10 extra-base hits.
Smith, meanwhile, notched 41 saves and struck out 107 batters over 74 innings this season for the Guardians.
Fernando Tatis Jr. moved up three points between the last update and now. Tatis Jr., before the start of the playoffs, hit five home runs and nine extra-base hits in the last 15 games of the regular season for San Diego.
Elly De La Cruz, who had eight extra-base hits in the final two weeks, moved to 87 OVR, a +2 OVR increase. He moved there, along with NL Wild Card hero Michael Harris II.
As for who went down, Yandy Diaz and Jacob deGrom were both downgraded from Diamond status.

Last week, Alex Vesia made sure to take in the scene.
A full month of baseball, he and the Dodgers hope, still lies ahead this October. Their game last Thursday was nothing more than a regular-season home finale, with the club set to open its postseason back at Dodger Stadium on Saturday in the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
Still, Vesia couldn’t help but feel sentimental as he traversed the clubhouse that afternoon, and sat out in the bullpen with several longtime teammates that night.
For the last six years, this has been home for the left-handed reliever.
As a pending free agent this offseason, it might not be much longer.
“I sent a text in our family group chat that was like, ‘I potentially could have played my last home game as a Dodger, in the regular season,’” Vesia recounted to the California Post this week. “And it was just like, damn.”
Vesia might not be one of the biggest stars of the Dodgers’ modern-day dynasty. But few players have been more important, or reliable, in their ascent to superteam status.
Since arriving as a little-known trade acquisition in February 2021 (acquired from the Miami Marlins, along with Kyle Hurt, in exchange for Dylan Floro), Vesia has been a stalwart in the Dodgers’ bullpen.
He has made 367 appearances for the club, a whopping 150 more than any other Dodgers pitcher in that span (Evan Phillips is next closest at 232). He has posted a 2.66 ERA and 5.7 wins above replacement, according to Fangraphs (ranking fifth among all left-handed relievers in the majors in that latter category during that period).
It was a rise that required personal reinvention, with the former 17th-round draft pick raising his arm slot and cultivating one of baseball’s most deceptive fastballs with the help of the organization’s highly-touted pitching department.
It was a road full of glorious highs, including two World Series championships, and gut-wrenching lows –– both on the field, like when he was optioned to the minor leagues for part of 2023, but especially off of it, after the unimaginable loss he and his wife experienced last October when their newborn daughter passed away during the Fall Classic.
That ordeal has changed the 30-year-old, in ways he still can’t fully verbalize yet.
“It’s been an extremely hard year,” Vesia said, with a set of pink-accented gloves honoring his late daughter resting in his locker behind him.
It has also altered his perspective during what might be his final ride in Los Angeles, making every little moment something to cherish ahead of an uncertain future.
“I’ve learned, especially over the last year, there’s certain moments in life that you need to stop and take it in,” he explained.
Vesia, of course, would love to be back with the Dodgers next year, and beyond. His consistent production and energetic mound presence have made him something of a fan favorite at this point; so much so, a local artist recently unveiled a mural of him in Burbank.
“I’m very thankful to have spent the last six years here,” he said. “I’ve learned so much about myself and the game, just what it takes to be a champion. That’s really, really, really special.”
Still, this lockout-threatened winter raises even more unknowns than usual.
Thus, even though he noted that “there’s still so much in front of us” this postseason, Vesia has allowed some nostalgia to creep in too.
“Even with Miggy and his sort of goodbye to baseball,” Vesia said, referencing likely-to-retire teammate Miguel Rojas, “some of the stuff that he has said about this team, I also resonate with. Like, it hits me too.”
Entering this October, Vesia’s bonds in the clubhouse and, especially, the bullpen –– a group he was first to nickname “The Dawgs” during their heroic contributions to the team’s 2024 title –– have never felt stronger.
Since the beginning of the season, he has been effusive in describing the ways they have supported him in the wake of last year’s tragedy.
In recent weeks, he has felt the unit’s performance collectively click into place, too, with the Dodgers’ relief corps emerging as a potentially underrated strength in their bid for a World Series three-peat.
“It was just like, guys got out of certain innings where … you could just see them start to trust their stuff,” Vesia said. “It’s definitely exciting. I think our guys in the bullpen are catching strides at the right time.”
Per usual, Vesia has been a key part of that resurgence. He posted a 2.64 ERA with 74 strikeouts in 58 innings on the season. More importantly, he improved his previously faulty command down the stretch, walking just one batter in 11 appearances during September.
Now, he’s hoping it sets up a storybook ending to what has been an emotional campaign –– and potentially his impactful Dodgers career.
“The way I view things are a little bit different. The way I go about my business is a little bit different. The way I’m motivated is a little bit different,” he said, while reflecting back on a traumatic 12 months that have made his connections in the organization all the more meaningful.
“Ultimately, I know the job that I have to do,” he added. “But yeah, my motivation for this month is different.”

Will Klein will always have Game 3 of the 2025 World Series.
With the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays tied in the series, and the game barreling into extra innings, Klein threw a career-high four innings without allowing a run on Oct. 27, 2025. He had thrown only 15.1 innings in the regular season, and was largely on the roster only because left-hander Alex Vesia was absent.
Klein doubled his previous career single-game high of 72 pitches in that game. When the Dodgers came back to win, 6-5 in 18 innings, Klein was the winning pitcher.
Will the 2026 postseason hold another magic moment for the right-hander?
Klein hasn't pitched in a game since July because of right elbow discomfort. He finished the regular season on the 60-day injured list, and did not go out on a minor league rehabilitation assignment.
But he's already thrown "two and a half" live batting practices to teammates recently, up to 15 pitches. Klein said he'll throw another full live batting practice Friday and try to get up to 20 pitches.
Game 1 of the National League Division Series is Saturday. Rosters are due to MLB that morning.
"Definitely feeling better," Klein said to Dodgers On SI on Thursday's workout day at Dodger Stadium. "Stuff's coming out feeling the way it used to."
Klein's first full season with the Dodgers was an up-and-down adventure.
At one point, the 26-year-old right-hander did not allow a run for a month — a string of 10 appearances from May 8 to June 2. Then came July, when a string of five consecutive appearances saw Klein allow eight runs across six innings, lifting his ERA from 2.27 to 3.67.
Not only has Klein had a long injury layoff without a competitive-game appearance, he wasn't pitching that well before the injury, either.
Still, Klein said Thursday that "I always feel confident I could get guys out. Even if I was throwing with my left arm."
The Dodgers had arguably the best bullpen in MLB without Klein. It would be at least a mild surprise if he's on the roster Saturday.
If nothing else, Klein at least sounds healthy enough to be an option if another reliever gets hurt or is absent for any other reason, like Vesia was last year.
"From where we were to where we are now, it's been encouraging to see," Klein said. "It's definitely feeling better."

The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

- The Dodgers enter October seeking a third straight World Series title, but the club has not settled on a closer despite spending heavily on Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott.
- Andrew Friedman is confident about the Dodgers’ bullpen adapting to late-inning, high-leverage situations in the playoffs no matter who might be called upon.
SAN FRANCISCO — Stop me if you’ve heard this a million times, but the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win three consecutive World Series championships since the New York Yankees, from 1998 to 2000.
Those Yankees had a Hall of Fame closer. In 1998, Mariano Rivera got the final four outs of the clincher. In 1999, he got the final four outs. In 2000, he got the final three outs.
These Dodgers? Their closer? Your guess is as good as theirs.
“I do not know,” said Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers’ president of baseball operations.
This might be a good time to know, no? The regular season is over. The postseason is upon us.
Alex Call hits a run-scoring double and Andy Pages follows with a three-run home run in the 10th inning of the Dodgers’ 5-1 win over the San Francisco Giants.
“I feel very confident that we’re going to be going into October with arguably the deepest and best pitching staff that we’ve had,” he said. “Exactly what their roles will be and how things will be ordered, I don’t know right now.”
Perhaps the Dodgers are overthinking this. They have done that before.
Tanner Scott converted 25 of 29 save opportunities this season, including saves Friday and Saturday.
But the strongest hitters on the Dodgers’ possible division series opponents are left-handed — Matt Olson, Drake Baldwin and Michael Harris II on the Atlanta Braves; Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber on the Philadelphia Phillies — and the Dodgers may not hesitate to use the left-handed Scott against those guys in the seventh or eighth inning.
In theory, these Dodgers have three candidates as closer: Scott, their marquee closer signing for 2025 and actual closer for most of 2026; Edwin Díaz, their marquee closer signing for 2026; and Roki Sasaki, their accidental closer last October.
Yet Friedman said he could envision scenarios where Evan Phillips could close, or even Brock Stewart, or perhaps Alex Vesia against a run of left-handed hitters. The Dodgers hope to activate Edgardo Henriquez for the playoffs. The starters could close, too, especially a well-rested Tyler Glasnow early in the first round.
Dave Roberts know the Dodgers’ chances of a three-peat rest on a surprise hero giving the team a timely boost. Meet Bill Plaschke’s top candidates for the job.
“We’ve got a number of guys that we really trust,” Friedman said. “Depending on who we’re playing, how deep our starter goes, there are a lot of factors that would go into it. But, more than who will be that pitcher on the mound, is the fact that we have so many candidates we feel really good about.”
That the Dodgers have improvised an October relief corps, transformed a rookie starter into a postseason closer and run bullpen games in elimination games might lead you to conclude Friedman does not really believe in the concept of a designated closer. In a world where “high leverage” is the trendy jargon, maybe a closer is more of an anachronism than a necessity.
That the Dodgers invested $72 million in Scott and $69 million in Díaz in consecutive winters would lead you to conclude Friedman does indeed believe in the concept of a designated closer. In fact, he does.
“I think it’s extremely helpful,” he said.
The Dodgers do not hold splashy news conferences to introduce closer candidates. When the Dodgers introduced Díaz last December, Friedman proudly introduced the three-time All-Star as the closer.
“For us, we have a high bar,” Friedman said then. “To name someone the closer, you have to be one of the best. You have to be elite and dominant at what you do.”
Díaz’s season went awry, limited to 18⅔ innings after elbow surgery and then a neck injury. But in five September appearances since his activation from the injured list, he gave up no runs and one hit in five innings, striking out nine of the 17 batters he faced. (In the same span, Scott has given up no runs and two hits in five innings, striking out nine of the 19 batters he faced.)
“What we’ve seen out of Díaz recently has been really encouraging,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “What that ultimately means, we don’t know yet.
“Of course, if you have a reliever who is really hot in October, that can be extremely valuable. It doesn’t mean you use him exclusively in the ninth. But, by and large, that’s how you would use him.”
Roberts saluted Díaz for working hard to get back to an uncertain assignment.
“I’m really proud of Edwin, given the deal he signed, to work it out, to go to the minors, to come back and pitch in whatever role we ask of him, that shows a lot of character,” Roberts said.
“He could have mailed this year in. That’s something that has not gone unnoticed. And we’ll see how October plays out.”
The Dodgers could be forgiven for believing it will all work out in the end. Their final pitcher in each of the World Series clinchers under Friedman, all starters: Julio Urías in 2020, Walker Buehler in 2024, Yoshinobu Yamamoto in 2025.
The pitchers to record a postseason save in those championship seasons: Kenley Jansen, Joe Kelly, Brusdar Graterol, Blake Treinen and Urias in 2020; Alex Vesia, Treinen and Buehler in 2024; Glasnow, Sasaki and Treinen in 2025.
The organizational flexibility can lead to some uncomfortable discussions within the clubhouse, as Roberts and coaches keep the relievers updated on the latest plan for how they might be used.
“It is tricky,” Roberts said. “These are constant conversations. They are ever-evolving. They are ongoing.”
If all goes right for the Dodgers, those conversations will be ongoing for another month.

For nine-plus innings, the Dodgers and Giants couldn’t buy a hit with a runner in scoring position, but in the tenth, the Dodgers broke through for a 5-1 win. Alex Call and Andy Pages recorded two-out hits, a double, and a three-run shot to give the Dodgers their first lead in this game and the only one they’d need.
Dodgers find their breakthrough in extras to beat the Giants
Making a habit out of squandering chances through nine innings, the Dodgers scored four in extras to beat the Giants
Before getting to that point of being tied in extras, Jack Dreyer did a reasonable job of keeping the Giants at bay as an opener, but a stolen base allowed the opportunity for just a pair of singles to open the scoring in the second. Shay Whitcomb singled and stole second, later driven in by Scott Bandura—his first RBI of the season, playing in just his 13th big league game. Bandura also tried to steal a base, but this time Dreyer was alert to the danger and picked him off.
Facing a traditional bullpen game with Carson Seymour completing just one inning to open this one, the Dodgers first threatened to score in the third, the inning marked by Tony Vitello’s ejection. With two on and a 2-2 count to Mookie Betts, a check swing in which he probably went around was called a no-swing. Vitello came out to argue what had already been a topic of frustration earlier in the game and was thrown out for the seventh time in his 2026. The Giants, however, got out of the jam, as Betts struck out on the next pitch, and Sam Hentges also punched out Freddie Freeman.
What the Dodgers offense couldn’t do in the third, it did in the following frame. Kyle Tucker got on to leadoff the inning thanks to a defensive error by the second baseman and moved to third on a Max Muncy double—his 27th of the season, setting a new career high in a single season. With two on and one out, Andy Pages evened the score with a sacrifice fly.
Through the following innings, the Dodgers kept threatening but never coming through, first with a Freddie Freeman hit with a man on being taken away by a great defensive play from Jonah Cox—somewhat redeeming himself for the error that contributed to the Dodgers’ first run. That, by the way, would be Freeman’s last action in the game, replaced after five by Kiké Hernández as Dave Roberts rotated key pieces.
In the sixth, Muncy nearly wrote another chapter in his book as a giant killer. But the deepest part of the park was just deep enough to keep him from a solo shot in a ball that would’ve gone out in 23 of 30 stadiums. Perhaps the biggest squandered chance, though, came in the seventh and eighth when the Dodgers first stranded a leadoff double by Tommy Edman with three straight groundouts—an inning later, after Muncy secured his third hit of the day, Andy Pages hit into an inning-ending double play with two on and one out.
The Dodgers’ pitching was the reason the offense kept getting these opportunities to take the lead. Justin Wrobleski was the first pitcher out of the bullpen for the Dodgers, but looking for an even distribution of workload, he only completed two scoreless innings in under 30 pitches. Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz combined to strike out three, each with a scoreless frame.
Although Wrobleski had a couple of scares, the Giants truly came back to threaten again in the seventh when Bobby Miller took the mound, but also without actually breaking through. With runners at the corners and no outs, Miller secured a strikeout, then lucked into Marcelo Mayer staying at third on a wild pitch quickly recovered by Hunter Feduccia, recorded another punchout, and finished off the inning with a groundout.
With both teams exhausting new ways of threatening without actually scoring, the Giants looked like they’d take the lead with a leadoff bomb in the eighth by Christian Koss. However, the call on the field of a home run was overturned when replay made it clear it was a foul ball, and the score remained 1-1 through nine innings.
Even in the tenth, it looked like the Dodgers were going to strand the ghost runner after their first two hitters were retired without him advancing to third, but Call came through, and an intentional walk later, Pages had the big hit of the game. With the four RBI he recorded in this game, Pages left Ohtani behind and isolated himself as the Dodgers’ RBI leader this season, with 85.
Sunday particulars
Home run: Andy Pages (23)
WP —Alex Vesia (3-1): 1 IP, 1 hit, 1 strikeout
LP —Duncan Davitt (0-1):1 IP, 2 hits, 4 runs, 3 earned runs, 1 walk
Up next
The Dodgers get a little under a week off before they get back on the field on Saturday at home. They’ll be playing host to the winner of the Wild Card round between the Braves and Phillies in game 1 of the NLDS. No starters have been announced for that series.

Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts did not mince his words when talking about Edwin Díaz during his mid-September rehab assignment. "He needs to pitch better. It hasn't been good," said Roberts.
Diaz, who has the highest average annual value in MLB relief pitcher history ($23M), struggled in the first four appearances of his rehab assignment. He had thrown just 40 of 86 pitches for strikes in his first four games with Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Diaz's fourth appearance was especially worrying. He threw 30 pitches — just 13 of them for strikes — walked three batters and allowed five runs. Diaz rehab came in the Pacific Coast League, which is notorious for being the most hitter-friendly league in all of baseball. That atrocious outing came in Sugar Land, however, which is the most pitcher-friendly venue in the PCL.
When the Dodgers activated Diaz from the injured list, Roberts revealed he'd be used in low-leverage situations. Well, he has been perfectly fine in his three low-leverage outings since September 18, which has assuaged some of the Dodgers fans panic levels.
Should Dodgers fans buy into Edwin Diaz’s success?
Diaz has only allowed one hit since returning from the IL. The Dodgers, however, had a run margin of +19 in those three games.
“The way he’s throwing, the ninth is possible, yes,” said Roberts after the Dodgers 7-0 win over the Padres on September 22.
The Dodgers will almost certainly give Diaz another opportunity against the San Diego Padres on Thursday. The current home series against the Friars will be Diaz's last opportunity to pitch against a playoff team before the postseason begins.
The Dodgers are currently without Emmet Sheehan, Edgardo Henriquez, Will Klein, and Eric Lauer. Outside of Alex Vesia, the rest of the bullpen is incredibly shaky. Tanner Scott has a 5.40 ERA so far this month, Justin Wrobleski has not improved since being moved to the bullpen, and who knows what Blake Treinen has left in the tank?
Dodgers fans should get accustomed to seeing Diaz the rest of the season. He's quite possibly the linchpin to this team going deep in the playoffs with the way this bullpen looks right now. Dodgers fans have the right to remain skeptical that Diaz will return to the optimal version of himself,

LOS ANGELES — Last year at this time, Evan Phillips and Brock Stewart were both recovering from surgeries and unavailable to pitch. They were around the team but unable to contribute during the stretch run and postseason. This year, both veteran right-handers are two key cogs in an increasingly deep Dodgers bullpen and an important part of their October puzzle.
Phillips had Tommy John surgery in June 2025, wiping out the last half of last season and the first half of this one. When he returned from the injured list in July, the Dodgers were cautious in his usage, not using him on back-to-back days for his first four weeks, and used him on one day rest only four times during that stretch.
The results were spotty at first, allowing runs in five of his first seven appearances, including an uncharacteristic four home runs in such a short span. Since then, Phillips has allowed runs in only three of his last 21 appearances, and the lone home run surrendered was last Monday to Elly De La Cruz, which seems to be a rite of passage for everybody these days.
“Evan as you would expect, the first handful of outings were inconsistent coming off Tommy John, but I’d say the last [few] have been kind of who he is, and it’s been fun to see,” manager Dave Roberts said recently. “There’s a two-seamer, there’s a four-seamer, and some sweepers getting some awkward swings, some chase. That’s been good, and his command has been a lot better, too.”
Phillips in his 28 games has 28 strikeouts against only three unintentional walks. Since the start of August, the Dodgers have used Phillips more aggressively, pitching on back-to-back days five times, and he pitched three times in four days in three different stretches, and during that span has a 2.30 ERA and 2.46 FIP.
“I appreciate what they’ve done, trying to build me up, plus also protect me, plus giving me advantageous lanes while also challenging me,” Phillips said. “It’s been great so far, and I definitely feel like I’m coming closer and closer to that best version of myself that I have been and continue to strive to be.”
Stewart, a sixth-round draft pick of the Dodgers in 2014, was reacquired by the team at the 2025 trade deadline, but he pitched in only four games for them before succumbing to right shoulder debridement surgery in September. This year the right-hander has a 2.45 ERA and 2.53 xERA in his 27 games, with 24 strikeouts and seven unintentional walks in 25 2/3 innings, including a scoreless first inning to start Tuesday night’s bullpen-game shutout of the San Diego Padres.
“When Brock’s healthy, he’s as good as anyone we have,” Roberts said Tuesday. “For us, it’s just trying to manage him the right way and keep him strong and healthy. He’s been great.”
“That’s very cool to hear. I just go out there and throw it, that’s literally all I focus on. But people tell me that my — you know, I throw five pitches, which helps as a reliever,” Stewart said. “They tell me my stuff is pretty good, and it’s always nice to hear that. But I don’t know, I just go out there and throw it, try to compete as best I can, and hope it works out.
Roberts wasn’t wrong. Since returning to the majors in 2023 with the Minnesota Twins, Stewart has a 2.45 ERA and 2.78 xERA, which ranks 10th and ninth, respectively, among the 576 major league pitchers with at least 100 innings over the last four years. Tarik Skubal, with two Cy Young Awards during that stretch, has a 2.50 ERA and 2.73 xERA, for example.
But staying on the field has been a problem for Stewart, who this season alone has been on the injured list three different times — recovering from shoulder surgery, bone spur in his left foot, and shoulder discomfort — inactive for a total of 95 games. Since 2023, Stewart has also been on the injured list with elbow soreness, shoulder tendinitis, a shoulder strain, a hamstring strain, and shoulder inflammation, limited to just 106 2/3 total innings over the last four seasons.
“I feel good, but I’ve told everybody though, one day at a time. I’ve been hurt a lot so I always try to take things one day at a time. But I’m happy with the way I feel, happy with the way I felt today,” Stewart said. “Getting close to the finish line, but happy with how I feel, happy with how the stuff is coming out. I feel like I’m in a good spot and can hopefully help out.”
Stewart has pitched in the postseason only once, in three games over two series with the Minnesota Twins in 2023. Phillips was an October stalwart for the Dodgers since he was acquired on a waiver claim in 2021. In 12 appearances for the Dodgers in the playoffs, Phillips has yet to allow a run, over 15 1/3 innings, with 21 strikeouts and six unintentional walks. Phillips missed out on the World Series in 2024 with a right rotator cuff injury suffered during the NLCS, and was sidelined for all of last October.
“I love pitching in the postseason, I love competing with these guys. In 2024, missing out on the World Series, but I tried to dig in on the fact that I helped us get there, and played quite a large part in the Division Series and Championship Series. Obviously I want to see it all to the end, and help us carry that trophy off the field,” Philips said. “I’m just as eager as ever. Fortunate that I feel healthy at this time, and just trying to build on that, continue to chip away, and be the best I can when it matters most.”
This season, only Tanner Scott, Edwin Díaz, and Alex Vesia have a higher average-leverage index than Phillips and Stewart among Dodgers relievers. Phillips and Stewart have each saved a game this year, and Phillips has done so in the past with 46 saves with the Dodgers. Roberts said he’d feel comfortable with either Phillips or Stewart getting a save opportunity in October, along with a group that includes Tanner Scott and the just-activated Roki Sasaki.
“This year, more than any other year, I think there’s more guys we feel comfortable closing out games,” Roberts said.

Last year, the Dodgers hardly used their bullpen in the playoffs.
This year, they would like that to once again be the blueprint.
In their bid to three-peat as World Series champions, of course, the Dodgers are expected to be led by their star-studded rotation. Shohei Ohtani isn’t pitching, but Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow are.
And if all goes according to plan, they will handle the bulk of the innings.
However, replicating the starting pitching excellence of last October won’t be easy. A season ago, the Dodgers’ four-man rotation of Ohtani, Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow accounted for 113 of the team’s 165 postseason innings (including relief appearances from Glasnow and Yamamoto). Together, they posted a 2.55 ERA.
It was historic production.
Which also means, it’s fair to assume some regression will be possible –– both in workload and effectiveness.
Thus, having more reliable bullpen options this time around could be equally important for the Dodgers. And while that might have felt like a daunting reality earlier this year, when the unit was banged up and struggling through the middle portion of the campaign, Tuesday night was a reminder that the relief corps could be a strength in this fall’s title pursuit.
“Obviously we’ve had a lot of talent over the years,” manager Dave Roberts said. “But as far as sitting here today at the end of the season, it’s as good of shape as we’ve ever been in with the bullpen.”
In a 7-0 win over the San Diego Padres, the Dodgers were not supposed to have the pitching matchup –– countering Padres ace Michael King with a makeshift bullpen game in a rivalry series opener at Dodger Stadium.
Instead, eight different Dodgers relievers held the previous red-hot Padres to a five-hit shutout. Along the way, several arms who once seemed like question marks continued to round into increasingly promising form.
“It was fantastic,” Roberts said. “This is as good as our bullpen has been, has thrown.”
It started with opener Brock Stewart, a key right-handed weapon in the Dodgers’ bullpen who began the game with a scoreless first inning, continuing his late-season resurgence after another injury-plagued year.
From there, the baton was passed on down.
Justin Wrobleski, who is in the midst of a late-season conversion to the bullpen for the second-straight year, escaped a jam in the second. Blake Treinen, who might be on the postseason roster bubble given the Dodgers’ relief depth, offered one of his best outings of late by issuing only a two-out walk in a scoreless third.

The highlight of the night came in the fourth and fifth, when Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz hung a couple more zeroes in what were important appearances from each.
For Sasaki, the outing marked his first since returning from the injured list and making his own late-season move back to the bullpen, where he could reprise his role as closer from last year’s playoffs. He worked around a pair of singles with two strikeouts and a fastball that, even after being sidelined for the last month by a blister, sat at 99-100 mph.
For Díaz, Tuesday was not only a third-consecutive scoreless outing since his own return from the IL, but his most impressive yet as he makes a bid for the playoff roster. He retired the top of the Padres lineup in order with a pair of strikeouts, and has now retired 9 of 11 batters he has faced since rejoining the active roster.
Asked postgame if Díaz –– the $69 million offseason signing who lost the closer’s job amid a previously dismal debut Dodgers season –– could still pitch his way back into ninth-inning duties, Roberts said it’s “certainly possible.”
“The way he’s throwing, the ninth is possible, yes,” Roberts added.
By that point, the Dodgers had already pulled away from the Padres. They mounted a four-run rally with two outs in the second against King, who issued back-to-back bases-loaded walks to Tommy Edman and Mookie Betts before Freddie Freeman slashed a two-run single through the infield. The offense tacked on more runs in the fourth (on another Freeman RBI single), the sixth (on a solo home run from Tommy Edman), and the seventh (a Will Smith solo blast).
In what was the lineup’s toughest test in a while, they passed with flying colors.
Still, the night’s most encouraging developments came from the ‘pen, which capped off the game with two scoreless innings from Kyle Hurt, then stress-free appearances in the eighth and ninth from Alex Vesia and Jack Dreyer.
The unit’s most trusted arms at the moment, Tanner Scott (who figures to be vying with Sasaki for the postseason closer role) and Evan Phillips, weren’t even required. Nor was Edgardo Henriquez, who remains sidelined by a back injury but still could return in time for the playoffs.
“We know we have a good group, and anytime we get to carry the load and everybody has success and throws up zeros, it’s special,” Stewart said. “That’s really hard to do, for all eight guys or whatever it was today. So yeah, it’s cool.”
With a smirk, he added: “Write stories about it.”
Come October, of course, the Dodgers will be hoping their relievers are the main story.
But if the rotation falters, the club seems significantly better-suited to handle it than it did a year ago.
“That could change in a day, in a game, as we all know,” Roberts said. “But right now, feel really good about everyone out there.”
